subsubtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT CATEGORIES OF AFFECTED WORKERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, given the Free Trade Agreement signed by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the statements he made yesterday, when he admitted there were losers and winners in that Accord, he unfortunately did not name the losers. I would have liked the Prime Minister to name a few categories of Canadian workers he traded off to sign that Agreement. Are they men and women working in the textile industry? Are they workers in the footwear industry? In the knitting industry? In the leather industry? In agriculture? In rail transportation? In shipping, in shipbuilding?
Mr. Speaker, I will conclude with this and I would like to know-the East end of Montreal issue, the Comite de la Relance is requesting a special grants committee to modernize Montreal's industrial East end, to designate the East end of Montreal . .. Now with free trade, the East end of Montreal goes down the drain the way that agreement was signed by the Prime Minister.

subsubtopic: LABORATORY CENTRE FOR DISEASE CONTROL-OPPOSITION TO RELOCATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in this great city of Ottawa the rumour mill is a stable industry and one of its recent products is news of the potential relocation of part of the Laboratory Centre for Disease Control to Winnipeg.
Ottawa has been the grab bag, to quote Regional Chairman Andy Haydon, often enough in the last few years. Ottawa Mayor Jim Durrell has written to me saying that any potential gain for Winnipeg will be a loss for Ottawa. They are both right.

October 6, 1987
Ottawa has recently experienced Public Service cuts, project cuts, language training cuts, discretionary spending cuts, total spending freezes, procurement decentralization, National Research Council reallocations, and over the last 10 years part of Employment and Immigration has been moved to Bathurst, DVA has been moved to Charlottetown, parts of DSS have been moved to Shediac and Matane, and the list goes on.
The Child Poverty Action Group on the Hill this morning stressed that the increase in child poverty in the region is alarming. Ottawa is not immune to tough times. We have bread lines and soup kitchens like many other Canadian cities. I therefore ask the Government to reconsider this potential move in the best interests of maintaining the total integrity of the LCDC.

subsubtopic: CALL FOR ELIMINATION OF CHILD POVERTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, why are people not enraged that one-fifth of Canada's children are poor? Why can we alleviate poverty for the elderly but not for children? Why is child poverty not a political priority?
"Although we say we love children, the only children we love are our own, and I do not mean Canadian children, 1 mean our very own, the ones in our individual families. Those children we are prepared to do a lot for, but not the children of the poor." Those are the words of Dorothy O'Connell speaking today at the Child Poverty Action Group.
Conservative MPs presently place the blame on parents, moral breakdown, divorce and alcoholism. These are not the causes of poverty. It is the lack of money and other resources to deal with the same problems that middle and upper-income families have. Poor children will not have the same opportunities in life. We must develop the political will to end the senseless waste of all these children who are condemned to repeat the poverty cycle.
If we love our children we must put child poverty on the top of the political agenda now. I call on the Government to make solutions to child poverty the topic of a First Ministers' meeting and the subject of an all-Party committee.

subsubtopic: EFFECTS OF POVERTY ON CHILDREN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, child poverty remains a concern in Canada. This is so despite the fact that the economy continues to grow at a rate of over 3 per
cent a year, unemployment has dropped to 8.8 per cent, and 260,000 Canadians have risen above the poverty line in the last three years. Our Government has worked hard to raise the standard of living for all Canadians. However, our task remains far from complete.
Poverty is debilitating, especially so when it hits our children. They are the citizens, workers and parents of tomorrow. Poverty robs them of hope for the future and deprives them of the opportunity to develop fully and express themselves as Canadians. In practical terms, child poverty means a higher incidence of mental illness and a higher rate of law-breaking in adolescence. We must pay particular attention to the problem of child poverty in single-parent families.
The Government has begun to act in these areas, helping to drop youth unemployment from 18.3 per cent to 13.8 per cent, decreasing the rate of unemployed women from 12 per cent to 9.4 per cent, and increasing the child tax credit. We must build upon these efforts and those of groups such as the Child Poverty Action Group and the Ottawa Council for Low-Income Support Services. Together we can give all young Canadians a real stake in the future.

subsubtopic: MANDATORY USE OF CAR SEATBELTS AND OTHER APPROPRIATE MEASURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate the police forces of the Regional Municipality of Ottawa-Carleton which have launched their annual safety belt promotion campaign. Their objective is to encourage 90 per cent of car passengers to buckle up.
You have noted, Mr. Speaker, that during the past year I have been presenting petitions and making statements on car safety, because present regulations do not meet the needs of car passengers.
To that effect, a doctor from the Lower St. Lawrence region, Dr. Robert Maguire, has helped me by distributing his own petition asking the Government among other things to pass preventive measures providing for such things as inflatable bags, three point safety belts and the around-the-clock use of headlights. The purpose of such a drive is to reduce by 50 per 100 the number of casualties caused by car accidents.
I have here, Mr. Speaker, petitions signed by over 30,000 people from the Lower St. Lawrence area and the Gaspe Peninsula who are asking for greater road security. I wish to congratulate Dr. Maguire for his initiative and to thank the people from the Lower St. Lawrence area and the Gaspe Pensinsula for having helped me in this campaign to promote road security.
October 6, 1987

Before 1 resume my seat, I wish a tremendous success to the police forces of the Regional Municipality of Ottawa- Carleton in their campaign to buckle up safety belts during the forthcoming two weeks.

subsubtopic: ELIMINATION OF LOOPHOLES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the former Liberal Government instigated the worst tax fraud in the history of this country with the tax credit to stimulate research in 1983-84. Marc Lalonde, John Turner, Pierre Elliott Trudeau and the Liberals made Canadian taxpayers lose billions of dollars.
At the beginning of 1984, the Liberal Government, through the Department of Finance, came to know that the tax deduction plan for scientific research was giving rise to problems and Marc Lalonde had expected that the plan would only cost $200 million. It did cost $3.5 billion and up to $1.9 billion were lost as a result of frauds.
In Victoria, a 28-year old mechanic registered in a computer course for beginners, launched a research business in data processing and obtained $5 million under the program. According to the last reports, he was in Hong Kong promoting a book on break dancing.
In Calgary, a businessman was granted $30 million. He bought two office buildings, a Jaguar and a 106-acre ranch before he also disappeared.
Mr. Speaker, Michael Wilson was clever and wise enough to axe the program shortly after the Conservative Party came into power in 1984, but the Canadians should be better informed about that Liberal flop.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to protest the sell-out of Canadian water through the Government's trade agreement with the United States. In return for an utterly inadequate trade dispute tribunal U.S. negotiators have obtained the right to future use of Canadian resources as if they were U.S. resources.
The Grand Canal concept of transferring massive quantities of fresh water from the Canadian Shield to the southwestern U.S. has suddenly become likely.
Robert Bourassa, who advocated this idea before the last Quebec election, and Simon Reisman, who lobbied for it before he became the Government's trade negotiator, are understandably pleased. However, the needs of aboriginal peoples, the ecology of the James Bay region, and the weather of central Canada are all to be sacrificed to the greed of U.S. water wasters.
Why did the Government not protest the flagrant subsidy of U.S. vegetable and fruit growers who pay $13 for water worth $350? Why were countervailing duties not used against this subsidy to discourage U.S. interests from lusting after Canadian resources? In the future will Canadians buy more U.S. vegetables and fruits grown with water from the Canadian Shield?

subsubtopic: CHILDREN'S NIGHTCLOTHES-INTRODUCTION OF FLAMMABILITY STANDARDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, over the last nine years I have regularly raised the fact that each year an average of 20 children under the age of 10 have been severely burned when their pyjamas caught fire and that one or two deaths have resulted annually from these burns. Last May I tabled a Private Member's Motion to require the Government to bring in new standards for flame retardant children's nightclothes.
It is with a great deal of personal satisfaction that 1 report to the House that effective this week night-gowns, night-shirts, dressing gowns, bathrobes, housecoats, robes, pyjamas, and baby-doll pyjamas up to and including size 14X are subject to stringent flammability standards.
In my view the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) deserves the thanks of Canadian parents for stopping another 20 children a year from being seriously burned and for saving one or two children's lives annually in future.

subsubtopic: PLIGHT OF EARLY RETIREES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to offer my support to those individuals who took pre-retirement leave from the Cape Breton Development Corporation as long ago as 1974-75. The purpose of that

October 6, 1987
plan at that time was to continue to employ the workers affected under a contract of service to the Cape Breton Development Corporation in order that they might be eligible to continue to earn entitlement to various benefits.
The fact is that these individuals will never be rehired by the Corporation but must continue to have unemployment insurance premiums deducted from their income. In addition, these UIC deductions, which in some cases date back 13 or 14 years, are taking much needed income from those Canadians who need it most. Conversely, other individuals under different and new pre-retirement plans do not have this deduction from their income.
I ask the Government to reconsider this unfair situation and treat these needy citizens with compassion and dignity. In other words, stop deducting unemployment insurance premiums from their income and reimburse them for the money they have lost.

Mr. Speaker, the challenge presented by free will have to be taken up by our youth. We accepted the previous challenges. Our generation and the previous ones have transformed this country into an industrialized, rich and modern nation. Are we going to ask your youth to rest on our accomplishments! It would suicidal. There is a market to conquer, a country to build. This is a challenge for our young people. They are just as intelligent, willing and eager to challenge the world as we were. We must give them that opportunity, the chance to think and act in terms of a continent and the world. Why limit ourselves to our neighbourhood, when our skills, qualifications and values are in demand on every continent, Mr. Speaker. Free trade is the future and the prosperity of a people, our people.
Experts from the Quebec Department of Agriculture have said yesterday, Mr. Speaker, that our family farm will not suffer extensive changes. I suggest to union leaders that they should not interpret the agreement in their usual negative way as, in fact, our marketing boards and other programs have been protected.

subsubtopic: GRAIN FARMERS-DEFICIENCY PAYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canadian grain farmers are beginning to worry about whether they will receive any government assistance by way of deficiency payments this year. Farmers have good reason to be worried.
After meeting with farm leaders in Winnipeg in August, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) strongly supported the CFA proposal for a 1987-88 deficiency payment. However, last Friday in the House the Minister backed away from this strong support. He said he might mention the CFA proposal if and when he takes the deficiency payment proposal to Cabinet.
The Minister says that he might have a deficiency payment this year. Why does the Government not act? Why is it stalling? After all, the Government knows the views of farmers. It has consulted them. The Government has some experience in putting together a deficiency program.
With each new day of delay on this issue, farmers begin to wonder if the part of the free trade deal which says unsubsidized grain will be able to move freely between Canada and the U.S. means an end to deficiency payments for the current crop year.

subtopic: SUPPORT FOR CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
SUPPORT FOR CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to commend the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Canadian negotiators on their successful negotiations for a free trade arrangement with the United States.
Free trade is good news, particularly for western Canada. It will improve the market in the oil and energy sector. Free trade will reduce input costs for agriculture while strengthening farm markets.

Mr. Speaker, it is with a great deal of emotion that I participate in this debate on the constitutional Accord, 1987. The Constitution is the most important document in our country. Our Constitution, the basic framework of our nation, is the business of all Canadians.
I am upset by the process that surrounded the 1987 Accord. The 11 First Ministers met in two marathon sessions and their agreement was presented for this Parliament to pass. Changes would only be made if egregious errors were uncovered.
The joint committee of the House of Commons and Senate held its hearings in the summer, when public interest is low. The committee should have travelled in order to hear Canadians from coast to coast. Instead, it stayed in Ottawa and only those groups that could travel to Ottawa were here to discuss the Constitution and the Meech Lake Accord. In my view, that was an extremely bad decision. The committee should have reached out to hear Canadians and generate more interest.
I, together with others in the House, had the opportunity to participate in the constitutional process in 1982. It was an historic occasion. Our Constitution was brought home from Great Britain and Canadians finally got a Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
I believe that the 1987 Accord is also historic. Quebec's signature on the Canadian Constitution is definitely a significant achievement. However, I do not believe that one should be branded as anti-Quebec just because he or she suggests that the 1987 Accord should be improved.
In a nutshell, the constitutional Accord of 1987 is not a "seamless web" as some have described it. It is not a miracle. In my opinion, it is a bad piece of work that must be fixed.
I believe that improvements must be made to this Accord and that the amendments proposed by the Liberal Party will not unravel the Accord. I do not blame the Premiers for this Accord. In fact, given the feast offered by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), the Premiers could not turn it down. I am sure they never expected such a bountiful harvest and I suppose that the day after Meech Lake the Premiers must have felt as though they had won a lottery.
In my opinion, the Accord is tantamount to a dark cloud which will hang forever over the federal Government. I believe the Accord puts us on a fast track to becoming "a community
of communities" or a "nation of shopping centres". I, and I believe many other Canadians, do not share such a vision for this great country of Canada.
Of course, some wording of the Accord needs clarification. For instance, what does "distinct society" mean? Is it limited only to Quebec? According to my interpretation, there are hundreds of distinct societies in Canada and that all Canadians are distinctive. Therefore, if the term "distinct society" means anything, then it should be spelled out.
Some may say that Quebec is not a distinct society, but Premier Bourassa thinks it is a distinct society and has said so on many occasions. The federal Government has a responsibility to explain what "distinct society" means.
Let me refer to a clipping from The Summerside Journal Pioneer which states:
If the people of Quebec can be accepted as a distinct society, then this should also apply to the aboriginal people of Canada, says a recent news release from the Aboriginal People of P.E.I., The Lennox Island Band.
"As aboriginal people of Canada, we are even more distinct than people whose culture and language comes from Europe," spokesman John Joe Sark said in the release.
This refers not only to French-speaking Quebecers but to Anglophones as well. It refers to us all. Our native people were here long before Europeans arrived in North America.
I also have serious concerns with the clause which obliges the federal and provincial Governments to preserve but not promote the French-speaking fact outside Quebec. My riding has a large Acadian community which is very proud of its language, culture and heritage. How will the word "preserve" be interpreted by future provincial and federal Governments? I believe, as others have said on this side of the House, that the word "promote" should have been applied to all provinces. These people have as much right and are just as distinct as everyone else in the country.
According to the Minister responsible for the Accord, only "egregious" errors would be enough to move the Government to consider amendments. It would be interesting to know who decides what constitutes an egregious error. I know over 13.5 million Canadians who have considered the failure to recognize their equality rights an egregious error. I am speaking about the women of Canada who had struggled with courage and determination in 1981 and 1982 to see equality rights enshrined in the Constitution of this nation. The Meech Lake Accord, specifically the Langevin amendments, places equality rights in a precarious position.
In 1981, after their long battle, Canadian women witnessed two legislative moves unprecedented in our history. One was the strengthening of Section 15 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms which protects all Canadians from discrimination. Second, at the end of the process, Section 28 was included in the Charter, which explicitly states the equality rights of men and women.
October 6, 1987

Now in 1987, it appears that Canadian women are back to where they started. There is a possibility that their equality rights are not guaranteed. By excluding women's equality rights from Section 16, the Accord renders the constitutional history of Canadian women virtually invisible. It is a rule of law that what is not included is excluded. This suggests a hierarchy of equality rights. Why are multicultural heritage and aboriginal rights singled out for extra protection when sexual equality rights are not? I believe they all should be singled out.
The 11 First Ministers contend they did not intend to exclude women, that it was a mere oversight. We all know how well good intentions stand up in the courts. I refer to a recent Supreme Court ruling with respect to collective bargaining and the right to strike. In 1982, when asked if the freedom of association clause would allow for collective bargaining and the right to strike, the Minister responsible at that time said yes. Although not put down in words, this was his intent at that time. The Supreme Court of Canada decided that this was not the case, that the freedom of association clause did not mean the right to bargain collectively or the right to strike. The intent of the 11 First Ministers regarding women's equality rights risks sharing the same fate. They are too important to risk that fate. I contend, as have others, that this clause should have a reference to the Supreme Court.
There are pros and cons in respect of this issue. I have heard many constitutional lawyers say that the Meech Lake Accord does not overrule the Charter of Rights. Flowever, an equal number have said the reverse. Why not make a reference to the Supreme Court of Canada so that a clarification can be made before this Accord is etched in stone?
I am sure all Members have received telexes from women's organizations across the country. I have received telexes from a number of women's groups, including the P.E.I. Advisory Council on the Status of Women, the P.E.I. caucus of the National Association of Women and the Law, the University of P.E.I. Women's Study Group and the P.E.I. Women's Education Bridge, as well as many others. All of them demand clear written recognition of women's equality rights in the Meech Lake Accord.
In short, these women are simply asking that they be put back to the point they reached in 1982. Those who strongly believe that this Accord does not overrule women's equality rights should not be afraid of making a reference to the Supreme Court in order to get a specific ruling before it is etched in stone. This Constitution is the very heart of our country.
According to the 1982 Constitution, the establishment of new provinces required the consent of seven out of ten provinces, comprising at least 50 per cent of the population. This made the goal of provincehood very difficult even in 1982. Now with this Accord, every province has a veto. I certainly feel badly for the people of the Northwest Territories and the Yukon, the people in our northern communities who might
Constitution Amendment, 1987
want to join our country as provinces. The veto will make it extremely difficult for this to ever happen.
I know that back in 1873, when my province became the seventh to join Confederation, had that provision been in the BN A Act of 1867 my constituents could very well be American today, and maybe the Hon. Member for Hillsborough (Mr. McMillan) and 1 would be representing them in Congress. I do not think Prince Edward Islanders would have wanted that.
I can even come closer in time by dealing with the Province of Newfoundland and Labrador. In 1949, there was a tremendous amount of debate at that time among the people of Newfoundland and Labrador with respect to whether they wanted to be part of the Canadian fabric, the Canadian Confederation. There was a very close vote on the matter. I wonder what would have happened then if the situation were what it is today. There were those who supported Newfoundland joining Canada. At that time Premier Smallwood supported the idea very viciously, very adamantly in the famous debates of Newfoundland. What would have happened if he knew at the end of the day that nine other provinces would have had to agree to such a proposal, and probably for some reason or by some quirk of fate, Newfoundland would not have been accepted? I think they, too, probably would have been part of another country.
Under section 2 of this Accord "appointments to the Senate shall be chosen from among persons whose names have been submitted by the Government of the province to which vacancies relate". Under the British North America Act of 1867, our first made-in-Canada constitutional document, the Fathers of Confederation saw the Senate as a forum of regional representation at the federal level. It is important that vacancies should be filled as soon as possible. This new arrangement could become an imposing obstacle.
Let me explain by giving a current example. With the recent retirement of Senator Fred Rowe, Newfoundland now has a vacancy. However, according to the Premier of Newfoundland, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) refuses to return his telephone calls. So much for national reconciliation. Should this confrontation over the fisheries agreement with France continue for a lengthy period it is unlikely that both levels of Government could agree on a new appointee. Under this impasse Newfoundland could be without its proper representation in the Senate. I believe those who think that Senate reform is going to be easy from here on in, and those who advocate the Triple E Senate, are whistling in the dark. They are whistling Dixie to even think that Senate reform is now possible.
I do not believe any of the things that I have dicussed have anything directly to do with Quebec signing the Constitution. I cannot see them as being great problems for the Province of Quebec. We want Quebec in our Constitution. I think the amendments that the Liberal Party put forth in the House of

October 6, 1987
Constitution Amendment, 1987
Commons would accommodate that. It would be easy for the Prime Minister and the 10 Premiers to sit down and say, "This is not quite right, let us do it right now, because if not we are liable to be in a strait-jacket".
For the first time in the history of this country, it is written that there shall be at least one First Ministers' conference each year. No one worries too much about having these conferences. We have had them annually for the last number of years, and sometimes three and four times a year. What I do take exception to is the agenda of future conferences which will include Senate reform, fisheries and "such other matters as are agreed upon". I fear that under such an open-ended arrangement the Canadian Parliament will become more and more irrelevant. We know the attention and the high expectations that surrounds these conferences, those photo opportunities. They will be a regular feature, and practically any issue can be brought to the table. It is quite conceivable that the House of Commons will no longer be able to act on issues of national importance. In an era of consensual politics, these issues may be reserved for First Ministers' conferences.
I have already briefly dicussed the matter of Senate reform. It will be a number one topic on the agenda at every First Ministers' conference. But, as I already said, I expect that those discussions will be rather short.
I also wonder what happened to our aboriginal people when the First Ministers were drawing up their agenda. As I mentioned earlier, the first inhabitants of the land known as Canada again got the short end of the stick. They should have been at the head of the list. Our party has proposed an amendment. My colleague from Cochrane-Superior talked very passionately on that subject. He feels very strongly about that one issue, and I support him on it. It will put the interests of our aboriginal people where they belong on the list.
The second item on the constitutional agenda, includes roles and responsibilities in relation to fisheries". This is one topic that I have special interest in since I am the fisheries critic of the Liberal Party. This has caused much anxiety in the Atlantic fishing industry. Several groups appeared before the joint committee to state their case.
According to the Seafood Producers' Association of Nova Scotia:
There is already more than enough uncertainty in the fishing industry without adding a major political element that would recur annually, as proposed in this Accord.
I agree with that.
The New Brunswick Fish Packers' Association put it this way:
The very threat posed by the requirement to debate fisheries jurisdiction each and every year would create further economic uncertainty for this resource-based industry which already must contend with the uncertainties of large fluctuations in fish stocks caused by biological and environmental factors.
What was the response of Senator Lowell Murray to these legitimate concerns when he appeared before the committee? He said and 1 quote:
First of all, fisheries jurisdiction is not on the agenda of the future constitutional rounds. I think it is important to note that 11 First Ministers deliberately did not put fisheries jurisdiction on the agenda. What they put on the agenda was the subject of fisheries roles and responsibilities which is a much, much larger and wider subject.
Well, Mr. Speaker, what an exercise in hair-splitting. We do not have to refer to Webster's dictionary to find that the words "jurisdictions" and "roles and responsibilities" are practically the same. Therefore, I was somewhat amused to read the final report of the joint committee, and 1 quote from a passage on fisheries. It states:
However, simply to place an issue on the agenda is not tantamount to having it actually discussed nor does it presuppose reaching any agreement. The agenda item is not "jurisdiction over fisheries" but rather "roles and responsibilities with regard to fisheries" which is a much larger and wider subject.
Senator Lowell Murray could not have said it any better. I could even accuse the committee of a little bit of plagiarism. Obviously the members of the committee should have travelled to Atlantic Canada before they made those statements. No doubt, of course, Premier Peckford naturally wanted shared jurisdiction. I suppose when we look at a province with high unemployment, we can see how it is very tempting to take over the jurisdiction or try to get the jurisdiction of fisheries, especially when we are fishing alongside the French, and in light of the way that this Government has been dealing with France's overfishing in 3PS and some of the foreign overfishing elsewhere.
We should look at fisheries a little more carefully. We all know that these fish do not fly provincial flags. We know that they swim from province to province. I am not as concerned right now with the present Premiers in place. But we have to look at a Constitution which is there probably for eternity, with very few changes that can be made, if any, under this new amending formula. But this is one issue that seven out of ten provinces can decide; whether jurisdiction would flow at some point in time to the provinces and whether it would remain in the hands of the federal Government. It is seven out of ten. Why not the unanimity clause there so that if any province is being hurt, is not satisfied and does not come to an agreement, it could back out and it could scuttle the agreement? It is ten out of ten to accept new provinces, but only seven out of ten when it comes to the basic resource we have in Atlantic Canada-the fishery, the lifeblood of our people.
One can develop all kinds of scenarios as to how an agreement could take place. I am a former provincial Minister. I know how bargaining takes place at First Ministers' conferences, how the trade-offs are made, and how one gains support from one province, by supporting one's cause in another. It is very, very important. I do not want to underestimate, and I hope that no one underestimates how dangerous that one clause is for the future to our fishery. As fisheries critic, I cannot support the Meech Lake Accord for that reason.
October 6, 1987

Former Prime Minister Trudeau repeatedly stated, "Fish swim and thus do not respect provincial boundaries". At that time, the federal Government kept its powers. 1 live in Prince Edward Island, the smallest province in Canada. To a large extent, we depend on our inshore fishery. We fish next to New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Newfoundland, and Quebec. Who is going to be at the sluice when these fish come into Sydney Bight and say to a P.E.I. fish, "You swim that way, fishy", and say to the other little fishy, "You go to New Brunswick, you swim that way", and say to the still other little fishy, "You go to Nova Scotia", and then say to the other little fishy, "You go to Quebec"? That is how ludicrous this debate and the Meech Lake Accord are on this subject and on others.
We have made a number of recommendations and amendments. If these are supported by the House and accepted by the Government, I will support the Meech Lake Accord, and I will vote for those amendments. If those amendments are turned down, I cannot support the Meech Lake Accord.

First, I wish to compliment my colleague on a very carefully thought-through analysis of an Accord that obviously has more than one structural problem. I noted the concern of my colleague with respect to the fishing industry. Does he agree that the premise that is presented in the House is that first Quebec signs on, because if that is not done then we are anti-Quebec, or that Quebec is signed on and only then we will worry about the other problems. Does my colleague have a comment in that regard?

I wish to thank my colleague from Mount Royal for that question.
When we are discussing the Meech Lake Accord and whether or not things should have happened before Quebec signed on or after it signed on, I feel that they could have happened in harmony. The fishery was obviously put on the agenda to appease Premier Peckford because he had a long dispute with Ottawa regarding the Canada-France agreement. He wanted some way to get back in the good graces of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney).
I cannot see that as having an effect in the Province of Quebec. I would think that the Province of Quebec would be equally interested in having the over-all jurisdiction of the fisheries left in the hands of the federal Government rather than attempt to compete with its counterparts in the Atlantic Provinces of Newfoundland, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, and Prince Edward Island. Fish could be all caught up before they reach Quebec, if the jurisdiction were handed carte blanche-which I hope it would never be-to the provinces to divide up among themselves. In my opinion, they could never reach an agreement on how that division would take place. Even if an agreement were reached, it could be something like the agreement reached with the European Economic Community outside Canada's 200 mile zone. As was discussed two weeks ago in Banff, the EEC was having great problems in
Constitution Amendment, 1987
attempting to control some of its member nations with the quotas that were allocated under the Northwest Atlantic Fishery Organization NAFO.
I cannot believe that the Province of Quebec, or any other province, has to have a veto over whether the Yukon and the Northwest Territories could become future provinces. I do not know about the Senate, perhaps that is a little tricky. I also do not know about the equality rights, and no one else knows. Half of the people on the one side will say yes, Meech Lake does not overrule the Charter of Rights and Freedoms of 1982. Equally, I hear the same number saying the other thing.
I am glad the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) is here. All I am saying is that the Prime Minister and the Premiers should have that matter referred to the Supreme Court of Canada and have that ruling landed down once and for all. I know that my colleague, the Hon.Member for Hillsborough (Mr. McMillan), wishes to ask a question, so I will sit down.

I have two questions. In the early part of this decade, when the Hon. Member was on the government side, the then Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau, proposed a variation of the Victoria formula for amending the Constitution whereby there would have been three classes of provinces. In the first class, Quebec and Ontario would have been given a veto; in the second class, each of the other provinces would have to combine with other provinces constituting some proportion of the total population to be part of any approval process; and in the third class was Prince Edward Island because only it could not join with any combination of provinces to have an implact for or against a proposed constitutional amendment.
I do not recall that the Hon. Member for Egmont (Mr. Henderson) stood up and expressed himself as eloquently as he did today to take issue with the Government of the day, and to refuse to support something constitutional because it flew in the face of the interests of the people whom he was elected to represent. Why the double standard? That is my first question.
My second question is as follows. Am I to understand, and is the House to understand from the Hon. Member's comments today, that if the House does not acquiesce in the amendments that the Official Opposition is proposing to the Meech Lake Accord, he will not support the Meech Lake Accord and his Party on the floor of the House of Commons when that vote comes?

That is exactly what I said. If these amendments that are put forward by my Party are not accepted, I will not support the Meech Lake Accord. I think too much of my fishermen, and I had hoped that the Hon. Member from Hillsborough would have stuck up a little bit for them too.
On the first question of the Hon. Member in regard to Prince Edward Island, to be honest, I did not agree with that. I have always agreed with the proposal for seven out of ten. When it comes to new territories becoming a province, or

October 6, 1987
Constitution Amendment, 1987
getting provincial status, I had real reservations on the seven out of ten proposal in 1982 when I was on the special joint committee. If we are going to discuss new provincehood, for example, for the Northwest Territories and the Yukon, my personal view is that it should be a bilateral agreement between the federal Government and the party that wants to become a new province. That is the only fair way, and that is the way in which most other provinces joined Confederation. I feel that should be carried over in the future.

speechtext:
I have great respect for the Hon. Member, his sincerity, and his point of view. I was interested in his response to my colleague, the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan), because as the Hon. Member will know, his Leader has stated the position on behalf of the Official Opposition and the Liberal Party of Canada.
In the sense of a constructive suggestion, I am going to attempt to make a proposition to the Hon. Member. It is one thing for the Hon. Member to castigate the government side with respect to the position it has taken. I do not agree with the Hon. Member. But I say, in the interests of his own Party unity, that what he is saying is that his own Leader does not understand the issues because, regardless of whether the amendments are not supported or are accepted by the House, the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) on behalf of the Party which the Hon. Member represents will support the Accord.
Is the Hon. Member stating that his Leader is mistaken and does not have an adequate appreciation of the fishermen whom the Hon. Member represents? Is the Hon. Member saying that the Leader of the Opposition is incorrect and mistaken on the position that he has taken?

I have always called a spade a spade. What I am saying on the fishery and some of those issues is that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) is mistaken, the Leader of the New Democratic Party is mistaken, and the Leader of our Party is mistaken.
I can tell the Hon. Member for Annapolis Valley-Hants (Mr. Nowlan) that I do not agree with either of those Leaders on this one issue. That is not to say that I do not support my Leader in every other way possible. He is a good Leader, and he will be the next Prime Minister of Canada, and I hope to be there with him. I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, and all Members of the House that I have a conscience. I do not believe that it is a good agreement. I am asking everybody in this House to take another look at it. Let us make it right and as perfect as we can so that Quebec can join and we will all be happy. We do not want to be selling our fish or bartering this and that. That is exactly what we will be doing in the future. We may not realize it today or in two years' time. I guarantee that time will tell. Years down the road we will be sorry for that one mistake.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Questions and comments are now terminated. Debate. The Hon. Minister of State for Immigration (Mr. Weiner).

Mr. Speaker, it is with enormous pride and no small emotion that I take part in this historic debate, pride as a Canadian, pride as a Quebecer and pride as an Anglophone within Quebec, and pride as a Member of the federal Government of Canada which has had the courage, the vision and the will to make this great act of national reconciliation possible. There can be no question that the Meech Lake Accord will take its place henceforth side by side with the most important documents in our laws and Constitution. But it is more than the negotiation of principles, more than a legal agreement between Governments. It is a matter, above all, of the heart and from the heart. Like a heart it beats with the essential truths of what this great country is, strong and undeniable, irresistible in what it says and what it promises. We are a nation. We are united. Canada is one.
In coming generations Canadians will look back and realize, as some unfortunately today do not, just what an active statesmanship the First Ministers have accomplished. In particular, they will see the singular efforts of our Prime Minister and the Premier of Quebec. What they have contributed transcends mere responsibility. Theirs has been an active moral, social and political leadership of the highest order. One day Canadians will know it and recognize that this Accord could not have been reached with faint heart or equivocation. They will see that it took a complete conviction and a profound belief, belief in a shared future which is now possible; belief in a basic trust and goodwill between the peoples of this country with which the enmities and the bitterness of the past can once and for all be put behind us; belief in the decency and integrity of those who have led us to this new beginning. I share without reservations those beliefs, and as one Canadian I accept with confidence and with gratitude this precious gift.
I am a Canadian, and I am from Quebec. Yes, I am also a member of the English-speaking minority in Quebec. To some that might connote a difference, another point of view or experience from the majority. Perhaps. In mother language, obviously. But I am no less proud in my heritage of La Belle Province. I was born there. I was raised there. It is the home of my children. It is my home. I share in the understanding that Quebec is, indeed, a distinct society. We of the Englishspeaking minority are part of what gives it that distinction. But for our presence Quebec would not be distinct. It would be homogeneous and perhaps a separate entity.
In our long presence and relationship within Quebec we, the English-speaking minority, have contributed to the character of our French-speaking brothers and sisters as they have to ours. We are all Quebecers and we share in our distinction. So it is that I understand here in my heart the terrible emotions so
October 6, 1987

passionately expressed before the joint committee by Solange Chaput-Rolland when she spoke of her feelings in the aftermath of the 1980 referendum.
We voted for Canada. Canada through its central government totally absorbed in its will to patriate the British North America Act of 1867, cared very little about those who had openly stated their will to remain linked to this country. Promises and dreams were shattered.
As Madam Chaput-Rolland has said, it was a deeply troubled time for all Quebecers, a time of battle and of conflict. Afterwards when the battle had been won, when all that was asked was the warmth of reconciliation, the embrace and welcome of partnership, there was nothing; a void; irresolution; if not indifference. Quebec remained in a very real way outside and alone.

The Meech Lake Accord gives us to chance to change all that. It gives us a new start as a family and as a nation. A beginning, not an end. All of us in this House and Canadians across this country know that the Accord is not a perfect one. The provision in the Accord for an annual First Ministers meeting means that the Accord is a first step towards a United Canada.
The fact that the Accord has raised a certain amount of protest, the fact that Opposition Members do not support it and that some people are concerned about its implementation, all this does not mean that the Accord as such is bad, unfair and useless. It is quite normal to be wary when one walks where one has never walked before. The path may not be a familiar one but if we do not move ahead, we regress.

Fortunately we have a comprehensive and thorough navigational aid to help us. I refer, of course, to the report of the joint committee. This committee, under the co-chairmanship of the Hon. Member for Cambridge (Mr. Speyer) and the Hon. Senator Arthur Tremblay, has performed for the Parliament of Canada an invaluable service. The testimony they have amassed, drawn as it is from many of our country's wisest and most learned constitutional experts, jurists and senior statesmen, points broadly and, in my opinion, conclusively that most of the fears expressed about Meech Lake are either unfounded or unjustified.
I wish to address myself to some of those issues, in particular, to those concerns expressed by the English-speaking minority of Quebec, to which, I have said I myself belong. I know that this community does have considerable anxiety over the implications of Meech Lake. I know also that in some instances those concerns have been quite expertly-and wholly irresponsibly-fanned to the extent that they have become embers, if not flames, of alarm. The fact that those political opportunists who seek benefit by playing upon such fear will ultimately fail is of little comfort. In the short term their damage is done. Or it would be done, were the Englishspeaking community of Quebec less aware than it actually is of what really is at stake here. But it is aware and it will not be
Constitution Amendment, 1987
sold a false bill of goods. The community knows exactly what rides on this agreement. The community knows that this may very well be our only and last chance to effect national reconciliation. And, as Quebecers and Canadians, they are not going to throw that chance away. The precise text of the Accord states:
The Constitution of Canada shall be interpreted in a manner consistent with the recognition that the existence of French-speaking Canadians, centred in Quebec but also present elsewhere in Canada, and English-speaking Canadians, concentrated outside Quebec but also present in Quebec, constitutes a fundamental characteristic of Canada.
Three paragraphs later the text continues:
Nothing in this section derogates from the powers, rights or privileges of Parliament or the Government of Canada, or of the legislatures or Governments of the provinces, including any powers, rights or privileges relating to language.
As the joint committee has pointed out, the language and educational rights of English-speaking Quebecers are already entrenched in clear and explicit terms both in the 1867 Constitution Act and in the Charter of Rights. The courts of Canada have ruled extensively on this issue, and a majority of constitutional experts agree that there is nothing in the recognition of Quebec as a distinct society which will in any way diminish or dilute the constitutional guarantees already in place. In fact, the Minister of State for Federal-Provincial Relations says quite the contrary. He said:
It would be difficult to see how this declaration, this interpretive clause, does anything but enhance-the status of those minorities.
The English-speaking minority of Quebec numbers over 800,000 people, or 20 per cent of Quebec's total. As others have pointed out, it has a population larger than that of Newfoundland, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, or Saskatchewan.
It is inconceivable that the minority rights of these Quebecers who have contributed so greatly to their province and their country would ever be jeopardized by this or any other constitutional agreement. The very fact, through Meech Lake, that Quebec has at last found its rightful place in Confederation means that there is no reason, no desire, or no logic for the majority even to try to erode those rights. However, if they did, if tomorrow morning against all odds those rights were ever placed in doubt, and if the indignation of English-speaking Canada did not overflow, if the courts did not at once strike down the motion, if every institution and constitutional safeguard either stood by idly or broke down, I know that one individual would not. The Prime Minister, our Prime Minister, would not. He will defend with every ounce of his being the rights of English-speaking Quebecers, just as he did the rights of the minority in Manitoba or just as he will the rights of the minority anywhere in the country, and so will the Government. However, there is no need for that ever to happen.
The Government of Quebec will not discriminate or act prejudicially toward its English-speaking minority, not now,

October 6, 1987
Constitution Amendment, 1987
not when, after these last seven years of roller-coaster passions and emotions, she has so happily and joyously re-entered the family of Canada.
There comes a time in the life of all countries, and for Canada that time is now, when we must stop everything else and accept simply but profoundly to trust one another. That is the maturity of nationhood and the measure of citizenship. We cannot speak of Canada as a country in which to be proud unless we can also speak of it as a country of fundamental fairness, respect, and justice, and we cannot have those without trust.
Quebec has shown trust toward Canada. Quebec has accepted the basic decency and the sense of egality of the Canadian majority. The minority within Quebec can and must do no less.
What 1 have tried to say to and on behalf of my brothers and sisters of both the minority and the majority in Quebec, 1 also say to those who have somehow sensed a diminution through Meech Lake of Canada's commitment to being a multicultural nation. This is not so. As a member of a community which has for generations kept its faith and traditions alive in places where there were no rights, when the exact opposite occurred, systematic suppression, 1 know that no law or mere interpretation of law can ever destroy or diminish that culture. The experience of the Jewish people is not unique. If not outright prejudice and oppression, most minority ethnic cultures have at one time or another felt the persuasive force of the majority to conform to that majority. Yes, at times in our history that has happened in Canada as well. We have only to look around us to see the hopeless failures of such pressure.

And today, all of usv whatever our ethnic group, our religion, our colour, whether we are part of the minority or the majority, realize the unique vigor which multiculturalism imparts to Canada. We can feel it. We neither hide nor deny our differences, we celebrate them. We rejoyce in them. Our understanding and compassion are improved because of them.
The true guarantee of multiculturalism is the importance we give it. Since it is so important, the Premiers accepted to include multiculturalism in Section 16 of the Accord. While the Premiers could now go even further, there is no doubt as to the intent of this provision.
Linguistic duality and recognition of the distinct character of Quebec will not compromise our multicultural heritage. No other right or privilege of Canadians will be compromised.
Mr. Speaker, the adversaries of the Accord, and these include a few famous Canadians, have tried to oppose adoption of this Accord for various reasons. They have tried to find in its contents implicit threats against our institutions and ideals, even though these will become stronger rather than weaker thanks to a united Canada.

Is it weakening Canada to give the provinces an interim role in the appointment of the Upper Chamber of this Parliament? I could only think that it will improve the calibre of that august membership. Is it a threat to national authority to confirm the principle of opting out? That principle has been present, if largely unused, in federal-provincial relations since 1965. Is it a surrender on the part of the federal Government to confirm in the Constitution the right of provinces to participate in the formation of immigration policy? In essence, this does no more than confirm the relationship which has existed for most of the past decade under the Cullen-Couture agreement.
There is no loss. There is no surrender. Perhaps there is some measure of devolution of central power. Is this inherently bad? We know only too well the obsession of the previous Government and its leaders with their authority and what it did to our country both economically and socially. As one witness characterized such centralization, "anemia in the extremities and apoplexy at the centre".
Some three years after the election of this Government, Canada is once again a thriving and optimistic nation. Now Meech Lake has brought about an act of reconciliation many of us had begun to doubt would ever be possible. We are restored. We are rejuvenated. We are complete. That is why the Accord is so incredibly important and why we must willingly embrace it. We may never have another chance.
Professor John Whyte, before the joint committee, put it precisely when he said:
Those who continue to oppose the 1987 Accord after it has been accepted and approved by Quebec, must realize that they argue not simply against the adoption of certain terms for reconciliation, they argue to undo the historical act of reconciliation.
Madame Chaput-Rolland, speaking as always from the heart, left no doubt in any who heard her when she said:
Surely you know that if Meech Lake is to fail for whatever reason, there can be no more negotiations, no more justifications. If Quebec is once again to realize that it is more difficult to opt in Canada than to stay out of Canada, then surely, you know that the roads of tomorrow can only lead to another form of independence, but this time not chosen by any political Party in Quebec, maybe chosen and imposed on Quebec outside Quebec.
For once I take no satisfaction from the discord within the Official Opposition. It serves none of us. It benefits none of us.
As Members of the House at this extraordinary time, our task is not to dwell upon what has not been accomplished but to accept all that has, against such odds, been quite remarkably achieved, and to go on from this moment, for it is not an end to the journey; it is our point of departure. It is why we in this Chamber, irrespective of Party or ideology and notwithstanding our differences in other matters, should seek in this regard to stand together united and to seize the opportunity to build upon the Accord a stronger Canada, a better Canada. Thanks to Meech Lake, the people of Canada-British Columbians, Albertans, New Brunswickers, Nova Scotians, and Quebecers, whatever language they speak-will once more
October 6, 1987

stand united together. Thanks to the Accord, they and their children can look in expectation and hope toward a new and more promising future for themselves and for their country, secure in the knowledge that Canada will not only survive but will flourish. We, their deputies, should do no less.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to join in this debate. Shortly after I was first elected as a Member of Parliament in 1962, we had a tremendous extension of the rights of French-speaking people in Quebec to-the use of their language and to the protection of their culture through a whole series of studies, a number of important pieces of legislation being enacted, and the bringing back of the Constitution. This helped make clear the role of the Province of Quebec. In all those debates and discussions, members of the New Democratic Party supported the expansion and the extension of the rights of the people of Quebec because we recognized, beginning at our founding convention in 1961, that the accommodation of Quebec in a federal Canadian state was a necessity if Canada was to continue to grow and to develop.
At our founding convention in 1961, we recognized the linguistic duality of Canada. Indeed, our resolution passed in 1961 foreshadowed the Official Languages Act which was finally passed in 1969.
I would like Hon. Members to remember that in those years when we gave this support to the Province of Quebec and particularly to the French-speaking people of Quebec, we did it because we knew that it was necessary. We did it because we knew that it was right. There were no political gains for us in taking that position. In those days, and indeed until very recently, we had very little support in the Province of Quebec or in Francophone communities outside Quebec.
While we were taking that position, we were subjected to a great deal of criticism and opposition from English-speaking Canada and indeed from many people who supported us for our views on social and economic matters. What we did was not done for political gain then, and what we are doing now, I submit, is not being done for political gain now.
I remember in the debates during the 1960s the attacks and criticisms which our Party faced from all across the country and to which I had to respond. I represent one of the most ethnic constituencies in Canada. In my constituency, there are people from every ethnic group residing in Canada, although there are very few Francophones. They were worried, and some are still worried, about what we have done in our desire to accommodate and make more comfortable and supportive of Canada the people of Quebec.
When the Liberal Government under Mr. Pearson established the Bilingualism and Biculturalism Commission, we supported it. When that commission brought down its report
Constitution Amendment, 1987
and made recommendations, we supported those recommendations. Indeed, the minority report submitted by Dr. Rudnyckyj, a Ukrainian member of the commission, urged support for the language and culture of the one third of the Canadian people who are neither Anglophones nor Francophones. The first Member of Parliament to support the suggestions made by Dr. Rudnyckyj was my friend, a former colleague in the House, Mr. Edward Schreyer. That is our record.
In 1981, when the then Prime Minister proposed that we bring the Constitution back to Canada, we supported him. We did more than support him, we joined with all the groups, the native groups, the women's groups, the ethnic groups, the handicapped groups, and forced the then Government to make major improvements in thg Charter of Rights which we now have.
I look on our support for Meech Lake, though I have some reservations about it with which I will try to deal, as a natural outgrowth of everything we have done up until now. I resent- and I will put on the record why-the charge that somehow, by supporting Meech Lake, we are supporting a diminution in the ability of the federal Government to bring forward necessary social and economic programs.
There is no Member of Parliament who would be more opposed to any suggestion that we do anything to diminish the power of the federal Government than I. After all, we have a proud history in Winnipeg. It was the then Member of Parliament for Winnipeg North Centre, Mr. Woodsworth, supported by the then Member of Parliament for Winnipeg North, the constituency I now represent, Mr. Heaps, who forced in 1926 the then Leader of the Liberal Party, Mr. Mackenzie King, into bringing in the first old age security pension legislation. Mr. King had promised it for years but did nothing about it until he needed the support of the Members from Winnipeg to become Prime Minister.
It was New Democratic Members of Parliament, I among them, who, in the minority Parliament of 1972-73, forced the then Liberal Government to bring in legislation which provided for regular adjustments upward to the Old Age Pension and the Canada Pension Plans so that benefits would rise every three months as the cost of living rises. No longer are these improvements to the programs which are so important to millions of Canadians brought in only at the whim of some Government when it thinks it will get some political credit for it. I could not support any proposal which would reduce the ability of the federal Government to deal with social and economic needs.
It has been charged that the Meech Lake agreement as it is now will hinder the federal Government, restrict its power to spend and lead to the end of national cost-shared programs. We do not believe that and many of the witnesses, including many of the constitutional lawyers who appeared before the committee which held hearings on the Meech Lake Accord, did not agree with that. They said in fact that the spending power of the federal Government is now stronger than ever.

October 6, 1987
Constitution Amendment, 1987
Their views were also, incidentally and significantly, the views of the members of the Parti Quebecois in the National Assembly of Quebec when that Assembly debated this question.
The federal spending power means that Ottawa has the ability to set up programs in areas that the Constitution says are the exclusive field of provincial Governments. We believe it is a very powerful extension of the federal Government's power. The Accord, we believe, gives this power explicit constitutional status for the first time. It would allow Parliament to create a new child care program, for example, and set out specific national objectives for that program. The provinces would have to take part in and share the costs of such a program or set up their own such program. However, they would only receive federal funds if the provincial program was "compatible with the national objectives set by Parliament."
That view has been attacked by many people. One of the most vociferous opponents of the Meech Lake Accord, using the argument that the federal Government's power will be greatly diminished, is former Prime Minister Trudeau. He asked whether Canada would have the capacity in its national Government to mount new national programs. We say: Just a minute, who is this expert to ask that question? After all, before Mr. Trudeau became Prime Minister Canada had established joint programs which gave universal coverage for hospital care to all Canadians, medical care, and provided a greatly expanded post-secondary education program in our universities, community colleges and technical schools. These came about because federal Governments, Liberal and Conservative, said to the provinces, "If you will join with us in establishing and maintaining these programs, we are prepared to pay 50 per cent of the cost as a minimum. For those have-not provinces like the Atlantic provinces, Manitoba and Saskatchewan, we will pay even more." Some of the provinces came in to these programs kicking and screaming. I remember how the then Premier of Ontario, Mr. Robarts, fought hard not to join the medical insurance plan. However, the provinces came in and the programs were a great success. All Canadians are proud of them.
What happened when this supposed great defender of federal powers, Mr. Trudeau, was the Prime Minister? There came a time when the federal Government was facing deficits and they were growing. The cost of the shared-cost programs I have mentioned were increasing rapidly. Mr. Trudeau's Government then brought forward legislation which changed the way in which these programs were funded. It said to the provinces, "We are going to put a cap on the money we will pay for these programs. We will not increase our contribution each year by an amount more than the increase in the cost of living. It does not matter that the cost of these programs is rising much faster than that, we are going to limit the amount we pay".
His Government also said to the provinces that they no longer had to match federal funds for these programs. "We are going to give you this money for health care, hospital insurance and post-secondary education in a lump sum and you can do with it what you want".
What happened when that proposal was debated in the House? Of course, every Liberal voted for it. If I remember correctly, and I think I do, every Conservative voted for it. The only Members who spoke against it, the only Members who voted against it, the only Members who warned the Government that the provinces might very well decide there was more political mileage in building roads than in funding hospitals, were members of our Party, the New Democrats. Yet our advice was ignored, we were voted down, and what we predicted happened.
We do not need advice from a Prime Minister responsible for the biggest diminution of federal government power in the 25 years I have been here, and perhaps in the last 100 years. What his Government did at that time you cannot blame on Meech Lake. The blame lies squarely, as I have indicated, at the door of the then Liberal Government and the support it got from the then Conservative Opposition.
Yet this same former Prime Minister who is now so concerned about the diminution of federal power and jurisdiction, before he came to Ottawa as a Member of Parliament, before he became the Prime Minister, in his role as a constitutional lawyer, was very clear about what he thought about the division of powersbetween our Governments. He put it very clearly in his book entitled Federalism and French Canadians. That book was a collection of essays by Mr. Trudeau and he writes there approvingly that education is a provincial responsibility only and draws the following conclusion:
Consequently, if there is federal legislation to grant taxation money for provincial purposes, this legislation is illegal for the excellent reason that the federal government cannot by law have money in its coffers which it then claims should be used for provincial purposes.
So much for Mr. Trudeau's supposedly principled opposition to this Accord and the opposition expressed by a number of Liberal Members in this debate.
As a New Democrat I believe that Meech Lake continues the process of accommodating Quebec in a dynamic Canada. This agreement will bring Quebec to sign the new Constitution, and that is for me a very powerful argument in its favour.
We do not give unanimous approval to this agreement. We believe that it has a number of omissions and a number of faults. We certainly believe it was a major error to require the agreement of all 10 provinces and the federal Government in order for either the Yukon or the Northwest Territories to become a province at some time in the future. We believe the rights of the aboriginal people should be spelled out much more clearly than they are, including the right to a form of self-government. We believe the equality rights for women should be much more specifically spelled out.

We have concerns, yet these concerns about our ethnic communities, and others can be addressed in the future when discussions will take place between the federal Government, the provinces and many of the groups who believe their rights have not been dealt with in the Meech Lake Accord. Elowever, despite those omissions, despite these feelings, we believe on the whole that the Meech Lake Agreement follows logically on the process which began in the early 1960s, and we intend to support it.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciated the comments of the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow). He has served a long term in the House of Commons and recalls personally some of the historical things that have happened here.
I was somewhat concerned when he was referring to Prime Ministers. I lost track from time to time of which Prime Minister he was referring to. Some of the comments he made were not very complimentary, but I do not think those were meant for the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney).
The Member did not say how he feels about the consultation process with the provinces with regard to the appointment of Senators and Supreme Court judges. Does he believe that this is a downgrading or weakening of the central Government? Does he not think that the provinces should have the right to recommend people who should be appointed to the Senate or as Supreme Court judges?

Mr. Speaker, I have been puzzled about the criticisms made of the idea contained in the Meech Lake Accord that the provinces should have some say on the appointment of Senators and Supreme Court judges. I make it very clear that I am not a lawyer, but I understand that until now the appointment of Senators and Supreme Court judges has been the sole prerogative of the Prime Minister in office when vacancies arise. To be very candid, I have often wondered why certain appointments were made.
Let us assume that a vacancy will come open in the Province of Manitoba in the next month or so. The Government of the Province of Manitoba would submit two, three, or four names to fill that vacancy. I presume that if the federal Government were not willing to appoint any of those on the list, it would tell the province that and ask for other suggestions. First, 1 do not think that the power of the federal Government and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) is diminished. Second, 1 think consultation is a good idea.
1 take the same view with regard to the Supreme Court. One need only look at the U.S. Supreme Court to see how opposed judges can be on many issues. I am not at all convinced that all the common sense and brains reside in whoever is Prime Minister or Minister of Justice.
I foresee real benefits resulting from the provinces making suggestions. I can think of a recent appointment to a court in
Constitution Amendment, 1987
Manitoba which I am sure would not have been made had the Government of Manitoba had any say in the matter.
