Mr. Speaker, this debate on the Constitution ranks for me as the most important issue with which I have had to grapple in my first three years as the Member of Parliament for York West. I say that because this resolution will drastically reshape the way in which our country will be governed and severely impact upon our major federal institutions. Moreover, the Accord serves to define who we are as Canadians. This debates is indeed about our nationhood and about what constitutes a federation. This debate, in the end, is about Canada, its people, and our collective future.
Constitutional reform is no easy feat. Our history is dotted with efforts to change our Constitution, some of those efforts successful, others less successful. However, all were difficult and all were emotionally charged. Yet, the measure of any constitutional reform is not merely in its introduction but in the success and favour it enjoys among the population at large, in the affirmation that it embodies the spirit and aspirations of its citizens.
Toward this end, I am troubled by Meech Lake. After considerable examination and discussion I believe that Meech Lake does not enjoy the support and confidence of the wide spectrum of Canadians, nor does it inspire an enthusiastic and patriotic approval for the vision that it articulates. It is my belief that Meech Lake places Canada in more precarious waters.
While I am troubled with several substantial elements contained in Meech Lake, I am also uncomfortable with and

October 6, 1987
Constitution Amendment, 1987
ashamed of the process, which gave birth to this document. I would like to address my opening comments first to the process and follow that with commentary on the substantive elements of the Accord.
The absence of any true public input in the development of this resolution is a national tragedy. The package was not only assembled and hastily ratified in secret by the First Ministers, it was accomplished by marathon talks which continued into the early hours of the morning-two characteristics which are certainly not conducive to drafting the most essential piece of legislation governing Canada which is expected to meet the aspirations of all Canadians and the tests of time and circumstance.
To further aggravate the situation, the public hearings before the joint parliamentary committee were held during the summer months, the worst possible time of the year for any Government to encourage the participation, involvement and attention of Canadians. In addition, before the first witness had a chance to appear before the committee, government spokespersons made it painfully clear that the government-dominated committee would not be in any mood to accept any changes or consider any amendments. For once, unfortunately, the Government kept its word.
We saw the spectacle of individual Canadians and an impressive spectrum of organizations representing various constituencies travelling to the nation's capital to provide Members of Parliament and Senators with very moving and passionate presentations of their vision of Canada and of their dreams. All of these efforts counted for absolutely nothing.
Canadians did not have a meaningful opportunity to share their dreams and their wishes for their country. This is a staggering and remarkable shortcoming because this stage in our constitutional evolution as a nation excluded the very people whom our Constitution is to serve and protect. There was no partnership. There was no give and take. The process was secret and dictatorial. It was a take-it-or-leave-it proposition from start to finish.
This approach, unfortunately, also gripped the elected Chamber. It was regrettable that many Members of Parliament of all stripes responded to those seeking changes and improvements by alleging that they were anti-Quebec or by promoting the concept that the inclusion of a new clause or the amendment of a current clause would scuttle the entire deal. The language and strategy used assumed that if the Accord could not convince Members on its own merit there was a need to intimidate individuals into accepting the Accord's version of Canada. This tack was not only unfortunate and misleading, it also depicted an air of desperation and insecurity as well as an attitude which was prepared to tolerate glaring and recognizable shortcomings in the Accord.
I am fully committed to having Quebec's signature on our Constitution. I appreciate the desires of Quebecers to enjoy the
pride that comes with that signature. I understand the emotion of wanting to be an integral part of the constitutional family. Yet am I and others to be faulted for having passionate feelings about Canada? Am I to be faulted for having concerns about the type of country we are to become? Am I to be faulted for wanting our Parliament to respond to the voices of concern or the wants of Canadians to improve and build upon our strengths and foundation? Am I to be faulted for feeling that a constitutional package which is insecure and weak in the face of criticism and which would unravel because of some amendments should not be allowed to proceed until it is properly fortified?
We are talking about the Constitution of Canada. In my opinion, we, as a proud and dynamic nation, should not be content with a mediocre Constitution, one that is left unprotected from the attacks of unfulfilled expectations on the part of Canadians.
While I recognize that perfection is clearly for another world, we should fully utilize the unique window in time that this moment offers us toward ensuring that we follow our best instincts, that we seek to protect the rights of all citizens, and that we make all Canadians constitutionally relevant.
The time to bridge the gaps of our society through our constitutional framework is now. Let us not in a cowardly way dispose of difficult decisions involving, for instance, our multicultural character, our aboriginal character, the rights facing women or the rights facing Francophones outside the Province of Quebec, to future constitutional talks. If we detect wrongs today, it is equally unjust for us to say as a Parliament that we will right those wrongs tomorrow, particularly if one considers the proposed unanimity provisions in the current Accord. That is why I fully support and endorse the eleven Liberal amendments that were proposed at the committee stage and during this debate by my Leader and my colleagues. Without these modifications the Meech Lake Accord will be a weak and insecure document. Without these modifications I cannot and will not vote for the present Meech Lake Accord.
I must say also that in face of perhaps irresponsible allegations that may come my way in terms of being branded anti-Quebec, or those who will interpret my vote as a nonconfidence vote against my Leader, of which both are clearly untrue, this position is neither enjoyable nor easy.
I remain fully convinced, however, that these amendments are worth fighting for right to the very end. I believe Canada and, in fact, Quebec would be the better for it and these amendments would clearly articulate on behalf of what I believe to be a majority of Canadians a vision for a strong and united Canada, cemented by a central Government that would not be compromised or paralyzed in acting for or defending the national interest.
With regard to the specific elements of the Accord, while 1 endorse and view my Party's 11 amendments as essential, I am particularly disturbed by two overriding flaws. One could be categorized as the human element of the Accord. It is the
October 6, 1987

exclusion of our multicultural and aboriginal realities and heritages. Second are the elements of our nationhood as a consequence of implementing a concept of a distinct society for Quebec and a more aggressive decentralization of federal powers.
In relation to the human element, I believe the Accord fails to adopt and promote a full definition of the term "Canadian". Quite frankly, not all the people of this country have been dealt the same constitutional card, nor have they been equally credited with being a dignified and contributing part of this country.
The opening clause of this Accord only recognizes the French-English linguistic duality as a fundamental characteristic of the country. This is absolutely true but it is also very much incomplete.
I fully recognize the historical facet of our two founding peoples and how this country came to be. I value my country's history and respect those sacrifices and the courage which made it possible for me to live in such a privileged society. Yet the definition advocated by Meech Lake is not only outdated, it is primarily satisfied with only depicting our people's past and our country's history.
In my opinion, the Constitution must also address the present and future realities of our people and our country, without denying anyone their proper place. It must express the complete fabric of Canadian society and, toward this end, the Accord fails fundamentally and adequately to recognize those Canadians whose origins are neither English nor French.
At the very outset of the resolution it fails to acknowledge our multicultural and aboriginal heritages. I am indeed puzzled at the reason for which the aspirations and pride of close to one-third of our Canadian population were ignored and so clearly undervalued. I cannot understand the Government's stubborn refusal to accept an amendment put forward by our Party which would permit the opening clause to define accurately the term "Canadian", for it is only by recognizing the four cornerstones of our country's living heritage-the French, the English, the multicultural and the aboriginal facts-that we will capture the complete and rich essence that gives life to the term "Canadianism". Falling short of that definition is paramount to denying the reality which is Canada.
If the Government does not want to express that definition, then what is it to say to those Canadians whose origins are neither English nor French, and who feel the isolation of being left out? I am one of those Canadians, and I do not feel, according to Section 1, that I am as constitutionally relevant as my French Canadian or English Canadian colleagues in this House of Commons, for instance. I do not accept that while they can be recognized in Section 1 I must accept to be in Section 16 at the very end of the Accord, and that I must be thankful and patient because before the Langevin round of discussions the reference to multiculturalism was totally absent from the first Meech Lake draft.
Constitution Amendment, 1987
In defence, the Government has responded that multicultural and aboriginal rights are adequately protected by Section 16 and that their specific place in the resolution is not significant. However, would the Government accept a reversal in the order of Section 1 and Section 16? If the order is in fact insignificant, would the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) agree to open the Meech Lake Accord with the contents of Section 16 and place at the very end of the Accord the reality of our linguistic duality? I do not believe so, nor should he, because a separate reference to our multicultural and aboriginal heritage apart from that of the English-French duality categorizes and fuels the sentiments of second class citizenship in many quarters of this country.
When many Canadians look at this Accord and see that they are not provided with a dignified place to stand, how can we as legislators be pleased with such a fundamental flaw regarding the people of this country?
If we were to take the steps to rectify this shortcoming, what is the price we would have to pay? Would it cause the collapse of the Accord? Would Premiers who actively promote and defend multiculturalism within their own provinces object to such an amendment? Would Premier Bourassa walk away when the dilemma facing ethnocultural Canadians is perhaps the greatest in his province, where much of the debate concerning culture and linguistic identify is primarily focused between the Anglophone and Francophone communities, leaving those who are members of neither community in total confusion?
No, I am not prepared to rationalize the opening clause of the Accord as an accurate definition of Canadians. No Canadian citizen should be treated as a tenant in his or her own country. We are all owners of this land. We all love Canada and are prepared to defend it. Therefore, let our Constitution reciprocate to its people by profoundly and fiercely confirming our bilingual and multicultural characteristics in the opening section of the Accord.
In regard to the second aspect, the element of nationhood, I remain uncomfortable with legislating the concept of a distinct society for the Province of Quebec within the Canadian federation. That Quebec and its people are of different and distinct character, there can be no doubt. That Quebec has a unique culture which is and should be a matter of great affection, I do not question. That they cherish and wish to promote that uniqueness, I do not wish to deny anyone. But to realize all these things, by stipulating through the basic fundamental Constitution of the country that the province constitutes a distinct society, I believe is wrong and dangerous for Canada.
For me, it sets up two kinds of Canada. If Quebec is a distinct society, what does that make the rest of Canada? It is wrong because it places in question the priority of the term "Canadian" versus the term "Quebecer" for citizens living in

October 6, 1987
Constitution Amendment, 1987
the Province of Quebec. It is wrong for it legislates that distinctiveness at the expense of the other nine provinces and the two territories whose people also may feel, perhaps for different but nonetheless for legitimate reasons, that unique historical forces have led to a different brand of Canadianism in that part of our country.
I am troubled by the resulting transfer of that legal and symbolic power, and because the energies and actions spent in achieving that newly acquired status will be drained from the whole, from our country, from Canada. This transaction could perhaps show a credit for Quebec's political bank account, but it would leave a very large and looming debit in Canada's bank account which would only weaken and diminish the national fabric.
I also fear the consequences facing future generations of new Canadians who will be coming to this country for they will possibly be introduced to a greater provincial patriotism, stronger than that for the nation. In the proposed immigration sections the federal Government will withdraw from its reception and integration services for immigrants and pass this responsibility on to the provinces. Thus the Accord rather than integrating our immigrants as new Canadians will, first and foremost, create new Ontarians and new Albertans and would undermine the full value of citizenship which formulates emotional ties to the nation and the newcomer, and kindles a patriotic love of Canada and of country.
In terms of nationhood, I also question the spending power provisions that would permit provinces to withdraw with compensation from national shared-cost programs. Under such a constitutional scheme, would we have enjoyed a national unemployment insurance program, or a national medicare plan? Will we as a country be able to consider implementing and launching a national day care program or a national guaranteed annual income under these current provisions?
I believe that if we have to err, if we have to side with either a strong national Government or greater independence for provinces on the major programs and services that we as Canadians deem essential and very much part of our social and economic contract with our country, then the option clearly should be in favour of the former. If we want economic, social, educational, and health-related programs to work equally for all Canadians; if we demand that a federal Government meet the domestic and international developments that come our way; if we are to address the homeless, the food banks, the ill and the challengess facing our youth and our older members of society, then we cannot afford provisions in a Constitution that compromise the ability of a national Government to create national-based programs which are rooted in quality and equality regardless of where those Canadians live.
In conclusion, whether one considers the great nationbuilding moments of our history, whether those moments were the patriation of our Constitution, the establishment of our Charter of Rights and Freedoms, or the creation of our own flag and our own anthem, those moments were made possible
by men and women who not only exhibited a great breath of vision but also demonstrated the political courage to follow, and while accepting changes and genuinely involving Canadians in their dreams and their aspirations, pursued that vision to its successful ends.
Would there have been these great moments if our political forefathers, in the face of difficult decisions, had accepted a mediocre version of their vision by passing on the more difficult and unresolved challenges to future elected representatives and future Parliaments? It is obvious that if that were the prevailing attitude of the time, then these great moments would have been lost to the entire country. Therefore, let us not, as the thirty-third Parliament, lose this moment to put in place a Constitution which truly speaks to the best instincts and expectations of our people.
Also, as our sovereignty as a nation is under attack by such external forces as free trade with all its implications, let us not at the very same time threaten from within the sovereignty entrusted in a strong, national Government that is capable of rising above parochial, regional and provincial demands to speak up on behalf of all regions of the country and of all Canadians. While we should not and cannot allow Ronald Reagan to speak for Canada on the international stage, it is equally true that we should not and cannot allow ten, seven or six Premiers to set the national agenda for Canada. It makes one wonder who was speaking for Canada at the Meech Lake table. What powers did all the people gain through an enhanced federal Government acting on their behalf?
Finally, if Quebec is the principal concern, as is legitimate, how are we really encouraging Quebec to be a signatory to our Canadian Constitution? It seems to me, when I analyse a distinct society from the national perspective, that it forces the withdrawal of Francophones deeper into Quebec, the Anglophones into the depths of the nine other provinces, and leaves those who are neither Anglophone nor Francophone still striving to find their place. The result not only cheapens a true and full definition of bilingualism and a real involvement by Quebecers in the national life of Canada, but it also encourages and inspires the growth of a rival and competing nationalism.
I cannot therefore place my vote of confidence in Meech Lake. My vote in opposition is a vote in favour of a Constitution which would have our nation's unwavering support and confidence and a vote in favour of a citizenry that is all equal, living in a country that is united, strong, able and capable to withstand any forces tthat may want to undermine it.

speechtext: Are there questions or comments?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member has listed several reasons for his unwillingness to support the Meech Lake Accord. I wonder if he would indicate to the House what is his principal objection.
October 6, 1987

Mr. Speaker, I am not sure if the Minister was in the Chamber for my entire speech, but I mentioned three essential elements that I am troubled with and, in fact, with which my own constituents are troubled. I do not think the process that gave birth to the Meech Lake Accord included a partnership and a spirit of trying to work with the dreams and aspirations of all Canadians in a genuine way. I then proceeded to suggest that two overriding concerns troubled me. They are, first, the question of leaving out in the very first section the human elements that define what it means to be a Canadian. If we are to have an opening clause which sets the groundwork for defining what is Canada and what are Canadians, in terms of fundamental characteristics, then I believe as a Canadian, and not necessarily as a Member of Parliament, that there are four cornerstones that give life to the meaning of the word "Canadian". Those cornerstones are defined by four facts: the English, the French, the multicultural, and the aboriginal. For me to suggest that the opening section should define the fundamental characteristics of Canada as a linguistic duality, which is true and undeniable, is inaccurate and incomplete.
I urged the Government in Question Period and in debate, and 1 do so now, to move the extra mile and include those other two cornerstones in order that we may have a proper, full, and vibrant definition of what it means to be Canadian. In that manner, we will not allow a Canadian who is perhaps of Greek origin, or an individual from the aboriginal communities, to pass on to future generations the perception within himself that somehow he is on the outside, that there is a separate category or distinction between citizens in Canada. That is my first objection, the question of the human flaw in defining the word "Canadian".
Second-and the Minister was in the House for the latter part of my speech-I am most uncomfortable and have trouble with legislating the question of a distinct society. I do not deny the uniqueness of the linguistic, cultural, historical, and sociological perspective that Quebecers bring to Canada, that Albertans bring to Canada, and that other Canadians from other regions of the country bring to Canada. But to legislate in our Constitution a distinct society leads me to worry about what the rest of the country is in relation to that distinctiveness. I believe that that distinctiveness is arrived at to the detriment of other provinces. I believe that we would be able to achieve what Quebecers long for in terms of being a whole and an integral part of our Constitution without submitting to the distinct society section. The strain on the entire Canadian federation is too great to withstand.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I have a brief question which will allow a brief answer.
Does the Hon. Member believe that Quebec is a distinct society within Canada?
Constitution Amendment, 1987

No, I do not believe that it constitutes a distinct society.
I stated very clearly that it has a distinct character and identity, as do Albertans when one crosses the Rockies, or as do Maritimers when one visits them in their communities. In our country there have been forces which have led to different brands of Canadianism. I accept that, and I am prepared to promote that. As a Member of Parliament I am not prepared to suggest that Canadians in the Province in Quebec should be legislated as a distinct society when no other Canadians will be able to or would wish to have a distinct society for themselves within this country. The bigger question then becomes, if you favour a distinct society for Quebec, what does that make the rest of Canada? Therefore, are we not talking about two Canadas, two communities that gave rise to the community of communities which was rejected by most Canadians?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Not by most.

I listened to the speech of the Hon. Member very carefully. He began his remarks by saying that the Meech Lake debate in the House is the most important one in which he has been engaged in the three years since he has been a Member of Parliament. The Hon. Member went on to say that the subject matter defines fundamentally one's perspective of the country as a whole.
In light of the fact that he is at odds with his Leader and his Party on the subject, is that not more than just a difference of opinion on one issue, but rather a fundamental rupture between himself, his Leader, and his Party?
A huge rupture.

When I stated that this debate is the most fundamental one that I have faced, I meant it. I do not think we have ever had before us an issue, a piece of legislation, or a resolution that served to define who we are as a people, and what we are as a nation. There have been suggestions by a certain number of individuals that stated that if one cannot accept voting in favour of an unamended Meech Lake Accord, perhaps one would be able to abstain or not be present in the House during the vote. I am not prepared to do that. I would rather respect an individual who, despite my beliefs, votes in favour of the current Meech Lake Accord for his or her principles, rather than an individual who, as a federal politician addressing the Constitution of his or her country, walks away from that debate.
The manner in which I look at and approach this debate is not whether I am in concert with my Leader or with my Party, because ultimately the only difference that separates the two is essentially that 1 am prepared to stand with our amendments to the very end. I believe that those amendments are fundamentally correct and essential, if we are to improve the Meech Lake document. I believe that they are worth fighting for.
In light of those circumstances, I will not allow a Member to suggest that somehow I cannot feel passionate about my

October 6, 1987
Governor in Council Appointments
country and about fellow Canadians when I have been elected to do that very thing. I do not view it as a question of partisanship against my Leader or against some of my colleagues who will vote in a different manner. I believe that I have to live with my community and my conscience. I have to listen to the aspirations that I come into contact with. At the end of the day, I have to live with myself and make sure within myself that my position will be on the right side of history.
I respect that there are deep emotional divisions on all sides of the House. I am sure that there are members of the Government who are on the Hon, Member's side. 1 do not believe that the Hon. Member would rise and ask his colleagues why they are voting against the Prime Minister, the Cabinet, and the entire Government. I think that he will respect that those Members who will stand up against Meech Lake are not standing up against the Prime Minister, instead they are standing up for a different vision of this country. They should be allowed to stand up and speak up for that vision, and I make no apology for doing so.
Mr. Speaker, there are only a few seconds left. I wonder if I may be considered to have begun my remarks, and call it five o'clock? I would have the floor when debate resumes.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE ADMINISTRATION ADVISABILITY OF ESTABLISHING PARLIAMENTARY REVIEW OF GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL APPOINTMENTS
PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE ADMINISTRATION ADVISABILITY OF ESTABLISHING PARLIAMENTARY REVIEW OF GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL APPOINTMENTS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of establishing a mechanism for the parliamentary review and approval of appointments proposed by the Governor in Council.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I appreciate this opportunity to debate Motion M-39. I appreciate the opportunity that it gives me to consider the principle of review by Members of the House of Commons in committee of order in council appointments made by this Government and succeeding Governments.
The Standing Orders of the House have been revised to make provision for something in the direction of the action that this motion calls for. The change in the Standing Orders that was made in 1986 is sufficiently limited that it is important for us to consider the question further.
I regret that this was not chosen to become a votable motion. I think it would be very useful to the present Government, Parliament, and to the people of Canada if it had been possible for Members of the House individually in their own
understanding of the manner in which the Government of Canada should be conducted to have the opportunity to express themselves on the question. The principle is a very simple one. The principle is that order in council appointments occur in large numbers. Appointments to offices as diverse as judicial appointments, appointments of Deputy Ministers who do so much to direct the affairs of the Government of Canada, appointments of officers of Parliament, appointments of persons to such offices as the Chairman of the Canadian Human Rights Commission and the official languages commissionership, and so on, are of enormous importance to the good government of the country. These appointments are made with very little scrutiny and all too often end up under the cloud, or certainly under the umbrella which can cast a cloud upon the appointments, of the system of political patronage which has been basic to the Government of Canada and to parliamentary government. I will say more about it later, indicating why 1 think the principle is important and why 1 believe the Government should give serious consideration to the principle which has been put forward in Motion M-39.
Since the present context is important to the discussion, I note that two of the Standing Orders of the House of Commons dating from February 24, 1986 provide for, as is indicated in the headline, "Review of Order in Council Appointments". Standing Order 103 provides for the laying upon the Table of a certified copy of an Order in Council indicating the appointment of persons to certain non-judicial posts. I also note that both paragraphs of Standing Order 103 provide for non-judicial appointments to be made subject to some review by having the Minister lay upon the Table a copy of the appointment order.
Standing Order 104 reads in part:
The committee specified pursuant to Standing Orders 67(5) and 103, during the period of thirty sitting days provided pursuant to Standing Order 103, shall if it deems it appropriate, call the so named appointee or nominee to appear before it during a period not exceeding ten sitting days.
It continues:
The committee, if it should call an appointment or nominee to appear pursuant to section (1) of this Standing Order, shall examine the qualifications and competence of the appointee or nominee to perform the duties of the post to which he or she has been appointed or nominated.
The third paragraph restricts the time during which this consideration takes place to the end of the 10-day sitting period provided in the first paragraph.
It is quite a constrained review which is provided for in Standing Orders 103 and 104. Of course the vital point is that there is not any opportunity for members of the committee to provide not only advice but their consent to the appointment being proposed or the appointment that has been made. In effect it is a review without any power to reverse the decision or any opportunity for Members of Parliament to veto an appointment which could conceivably be a flagrant case of political patronage, such as appointing someone without any
October 6, 1987

real qualification to a position. Yet, committee members, having looked at the person, have to say that they do not think it is a proper appointment but they cannot do anything about it. That is the present situation under Standing Orders 103 and 104.
These particular Standing Orders do not follow the recommendations of the so-called McGrath committee on the reform of Parliament which considered a great variety of matters that have been implemented in changing the governance of the House, the operations of the committees, and so on. A variety of changes have been made to the better functioning of the Parliament of Canada and to the better conduct of the business of the Government of Canada.
The committee, in chapter five of its third report on the scrutiny of order in council appointments, looked to a more significant review than the Standing Orders have provided. The special committee's consideration of these matters reached a diversity of offices-to Deputy Ministers, to Crown corporations, and to regulatory agencies.
The committee was guided by a number of principles which I want to cite. The first one is that the primary purpose of the nomination procedure is to seek out and facilitate appointment of the best possible people. The second principle is that it is vital to the health of a political system that the public look upon public appointments as more than political patronage. However, the committee felt, as the third principle suggests, that there were good reasons for excluding some appointments from any political scrutiny process. It suggested in the fourth principle that some appointments required different degrees of scrutiny from others, so it suggested a diversity of procedures which should be applied to the various offices.
The recommendations of the special committee which looked at parliamentary institutions and considered reform of them, these proposals to extend the power of Private Members of the House of Commons to make the House of Commons work more effectively, are the kinds of principles I am pressing in this particular debate. To say that I am pressing them is to say that I think we should look a good deal further than the Standing Orders have provided and perhaps even than the McGrath committee recommended.
I am encouraged in such thoughts by the words of the Chairman of the committee who, in speaking to the Canadian Regional Conference of the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association, something over a month after the third report was tabled in June, 1985, had some observations on this particular concern. At one point in his speech in Quebec City he said that the movement to scrutinize appointments was symptomatic of the frustration felt by many Private Members with regard to their power vis-a-vis the power of the executive. He went on to say that while their recommendations represented a fundamental change in our system, they determined that they could not tamper to any great extent with the principle of the Government being responsible and accountable to Parliament.
Governor in Council Appointments
He went on to say: "Above all the Government must be allowed to govern".
I suggest, with great respect to this past Hon. Member of the House who now of course is the Hon. Lieutenant-Governor of the Province of Newfoundland, that the principle here should not have been that the Government must be allowed to govern, but that the Government should be required to govern in the public interest.
If that were to be the guiding principle, let me expand on what I mean by applying a modification to the situation before us of order in council appointments. We have an historical development to appreciate. We have the reality that government by the monarch or government of the Crown in Great Britain and in the colonies where self-government was achieved-and in Canada we talk about responsible government as the term for it-was a government in which the power of the monarch or the Crown was taken over by the Leader of the Party which succeeded in winning the most seats in an election. What happened behind the fa?ade of the Crown- and this is still in fact carried on behind that fapade as a symbol of the Government of Canada, of the Governments of the provinces, and of other government units of the Commonwealth-is that the Leader of the majority Party who has been successful in persuading the electors of the country or a province to elect his or her fellow candidates in an election achieves as far-reaching a power as the Crown is capable of exercising.
The responsible government reality is that these Members gather in the House of Commons. The majority forms the Government. The Leader chooses the Members to form Cabinet, but of course they are subject to our scrutiny and questioning in the House of Commons every sitting day. We are profoundly grateful to the parliamentary evolution of which we are now the heirs, that Members who become Ministers are here and are subject to our questioning day by day.
The Canadian House of Commons particularly expresses this practice in a vigorous way, sometimes in a way that the Speaker finds it difficult to control. Ministers do not have any idea who will be asking questions and what they may be about other than that they are sensitive to the issues of the day. They are, however, briefed on issues of the day. We have here a vigorous process of questioning of Ministers as to conduct of the Government of Canada. Though Members have their own opinions as to the adequacy of the answers given or, I suppose, to the insight that characterizes the questions being asked, Canadians-as our news broadcasts, particularly our television broadcasts, demonstrate night after night when the House is sitting-have a vigorous scrutiny of the Government of Canada.
Yet the Hon. James McGrath in his speech said that Private Members feel a frustration when they contemplate the

October 6, 1987
Governor in Council Appointments
executive, the Deputy Ministers, the Crown agencies at further reach, Crown corporations, commissioners and so on who are responsible to Ministers in the House, when we think of the various persons who are responsible for the implementation of the country's legislation, for ensuring that the Government of Canada is well conducted. When Private Members try to scrutinize these actions, they find themselves quite frustrated.
Here I want to recognize one very important reality. Though the Ministers themselves are here in the House subject to questioning and expected to respond to questions from other Members of the House, the Deputy Ministers, who are their subordinates, ostensibly in the nature of things may very well feel themselves even more subject to the Privy Council office, conceivably to Treasury Board. They may feel themselves subject to very few, persons in the conduct of government.
In the practice of our Government, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has become the uncrowned monarch. The Prime Minister, choosing a Clerk of the Privy Council and choosing with advice the Deputy Ministers of government and having a leading role in choosing others who receive order in council appointments, exercises his authority under a system that may not be very far removed from the reality of 200 years ago. King George III was active 200 years ago in Great Britain working to create a parliamentary coalition to produce enough votes to back up his Ministers and his Government. When we have the Prime Minister as uncrowned king making appointments which are in his power through the Cabinet, which he controls so largely, we have a system of government which may not be very far removed from the autocratic government, a government unchecked by parliamentary institution, which once prevailed in England before the parliamentary evolution of the 19th century.
Because we have persons who are responsible primarily to the Prime Minister or to the Clerk of the Privy Council-in the case of Deputy Ministers and other people who issue reports who occasionally may appear in the public eye but do not experience very much in the way of scrutiny by way of Members of Parliament-these are realities that have moved me to suggest that we look far beyond Standing Orders 103 and 104 and even beyond the McGrath committee and its recommendations for scrutiny. We should recognize the advisability of having scrutiny in committee that opens a genuine advise and consent possibility in which members of the committee can consider rejecting an appointment or advising against it or, in short, vetoing the appointment.
That suggestion will arouse concern in some minds because of the American situation. Members of Congress have far-reaching powers of review of potential appointees. These days they are considering a nominee to the Supreme Court of the United States, an appointee who may well not be appointed, though the President of the United States would will it if he possibly could. In those cases we see a most rigorous process of review.
The argument that I have been making on the basis of British constitutional principles applied in Canada and in other units of the Commonwealth is the development of parliamentary government. We can make an argument for this further development of responsibility and power, if you will, of Members of Parliament as individuals in committee. Committees will still be constructed according to the composition of Parliament. In the present Parliament that means they would be overwhelmingly made up of Conservative Members. That provides some safeguard immediately against any fear among Canadians and Members of this House that the worst abuses of the American process might occur. If we are going to have the principle of a genuinely responsible government applied to the appointees of government, as I think should be the case, then we need to take this one step further. Let me say very firmly that this a direction that I think should be taken. Our parliamentary democracy requires that Crown prerogatives genuinely be limited by responsible government. That means accountability of the Government to the people through their elected representatives of Parliament. 1 want to urge in the very strongest terms for consideration of these matters the question of how many of the order in council appointments should be so reviewed and exactly where they should occur, whether in a single committee or in standing committees which have expertise in various areas. It involves detail. Questions would have to be be answered. I hesitate more because I fear the possibility of its role being extended too far. 1 do believe that many of the appointments made are of eminently qualified persons. In those cases there would not be very much in the way of a review process to be gone through.
While hesitating to single out any of the persons who have been appointed by previous Governments or by this one, we all realize that there have been times when persons have been appointed whose main qualification was their membership in a political Party. In those cases where a person may actually confess to very limited qualification for the office to which he or she is being appointed, surely we have the strongest of arguments for having a process which may very well serve as a deterrent. Prime Ministers would be more careful in making appointments. If not, if they were unmindful of the necessity of the best qualified persons for these positions, let the principle of responsible government extend to those appointments. Let us have the power to turn them back and have people who are qualified appointed to offices.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE ADMINISTRATION ADVISABILITY OF ESTABLISHING PARLIAMENTARY REVIEW OF GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL APPOINTMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege to join the debate on the motion introduced by the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Epp) with respect to parliamentary reform in a review of governor in council appointments.
As all Hon. Members know very well, it was this Government that initiated at the beginning of its mandate three years ago what was perhaps the most sweeping action to reform the
October 6, 1987

House of Commons in Canadian history. One would wonder why it took so long for this action to take place.
Certainly that reform brought this place that governed our country for so many years up to date, brought to it a change that would give each and every Member of Parliament more ability to reflect the views of those in the area he represents. I take pride in the fact that it was the present Government that took this initiative.
The fact is that the Hon. Member who introduced this motion could now take it to a committee which he may have done to see if he could get a five-hour debate on it and to see if it could be votable. That is a dynamic change from what has ever happened before. That is a tremendous change and one that I am sure the Hon. Member himself has reflected upon and is enthusiastic about. Certainly I welcome his views on how he might improve on it.
In December of 1984, the Government established the special committee on reform to which the Hon. Member alluded under the distinguished leadership of the former Hon. Member for Saint John's East, now the Lieutenant-Governor of Newfoundland and Labrador. Under that inspired leadership, and with the diligent and non-partisan work of all members of the committee representing all Parties, the Hon. Member's Party included, the McGrath committee produced three unanimous reports between December of 1984 and June of 1985. These reports recommended a comprehensive package of reforms to the House and its rules. The principal purpose of these reforms, of course, was to strengthen the role of the Private Member, as I indicated earlier, and to give us a more influential role in reviewing the actions of the Government and proposing policy amendments and new initiatives.
What we have witnessed here today is of course another new initiative, albeit one brought on by a Private Member from the opposition Party. I think that is democracy in action, open debate for those in the House and those who may be sitting in their offices watching us on television or those who may read Hansard tomorrow. So be it. It is a point of view and the Hon. Member expressed it well.
These changes to the Standing Orders were tested for one year, as the Hon. Member may recall. I think one could fairly say that they passed the test with some modifications and were adopted on a permanent basis by the House, again with allParty support, in June of this year.
There are many examples of these reforms, including legislative committee approval given to Bills after House approval at second reading, and expanded powers granted to smaller and reorganized standing committees to review the activities of government Departments and the very rules we are operating under in Private Members' Business.
In addition, the Government and the House agreed to provide an opportunity to standing committees to meet with the broad spectrum of people which the Government appoints or, under the new House rules, may nominate to important
Governor in Council Appointments
positions in the service of Canada. I chair a committee. Before that very committee appeared the likes of Mr. Dalton Camp and Mr. Ian Deans, a former Member of the House. Quite frankly, those kinds of scrutinies of people to be appointed had never previously occurred.
Certainly that openness in which the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon participated is certainly an idea which 1 think has shed a new light on appointments in general. I have yet to see a motion before these committees reviewing appointments to recommend that the appointees not be accepted or that the Government change its mind. I do not think, quite frankly, that it has even happened so far. However, that device is available to opposition Members of these committees.
The Hon. Member shakes his head. Such a motion may not be passed but it can be made. This device, to my knowledge, has never been exercised. I stand to be corrected. I only chair one committee and appointments have gone before other committees as well.
This reform is of course the basic focus of our discussion today. The mechanisms called for in the motion before us really are now in place. They permit standing committees to review the qualifications and competence of appointments and nominations made by the Government. They are unprecedented in any parliamentary system of government.
The Hon. Member may watch on Channel 50 the U.S. Senate review committees. That is not a parliamentary system. That is a totally different system which maybe he thinks we ought to use. We have a little trouble with that.
On one hand, we are worried about our sovereignty, as we know if we listen to Question Period, yet the Hon. Member purports to move to a U.S. system of Government. One must be very careful and concerned about why he would like to change a system that is very uniquely Canadian, a proposal of the Government to which all Parties agreed. Now he wants to move us into a system like that which we see in the United States where they challenge the nominees and recommend, as we are witnessing right now, if the candidate should be allowed to be appointed. That is a very grave concern to me.
We would like to maintain our sovereignty and certainly not move right away into a U.S. system. The Hon. Member brought forth no argument to show what other parliamentary system of government is in fact going further than in Canada. He has no examples because we have taken such a tremendous stride in bringing forth a new concept and a new power for the Member of Parliament.
The election of the Speaker and the Deputy Speaker is a new idea, and we are still actually living and testing the system. There may come a time when we would like to modify it, but to move immediately from this reform into an expanded reform could, I respectfully submit, bring forth other grave problems. One would want to be very careful, especially when

we consider what is important and unique to Canadians. The Hon. Member's Party was very much a part of the process.
Once again I want to illustrate that the Hon. Member's ability to bring a new idea forward is one we are debating right now. speechtext:

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE ADMINISTRATION ADVISABILITY OF ESTABLISHING PARLIAMENTARY REVIEW OF GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL APPOINTMENTS
speechtext: Revolutionary change.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE ADMINISTRATION ADVISABILITY OF ESTABLISHING PARLIAMENTARY REVIEW OF GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL APPOINTMENTS
speechtext:
It is hardly revolutionary. It is a mild, modest, cautious beginning.
The Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Epp) would have this House introduce a system somewhat parallel to the U.S. model. Of course he is not in any way suggesting that we should have a congressional system or anything of the kind. He is saying that we should look at the U.S. model where certain nominations are sent to a Senate committee. I would point out that the House of Representatives has no part to play at all in this process.
The committee examining the appointment has jurisdiction in the area to which the appointment belongs. The committee considers the matter either in a public forum or, by a majority
vote, in camera. It then reports back to the Senate, and the question is: Will the Senate advise and consent to the nomination?
The McGrath committee, in looking at that system, noted that statistically there are very few direct refusals of appointments by the Senate. However, it also went on to note that it is not uncommon for nominations to be withdrawn or not to be confirmed at all. Why do you suppose that is? I think we know that in the course of the hearings the would-be appointee sometimes becomes something of an embarrassment to the administration. He or she has been unable to answer certain questions truthfully, with clarity or knowledge. In other words, their competence has been challenged.
The Hon. Member wants a review and approval process to be put in place in Canada. I fully agree with him. There is a need for just such a system. I believe, and I wonder if there are not many other Members of Parliament who share this belief, that political patronage in this country has really gotten out of hand. In certain cases it has actually gone wild. In saying this I want it to be clear that what is under attack here are not appointments themselves. There may be too many boards and commissions and the like to which the Prime Minister and the Government may make appointments. Yet some of them are useful, and some are essential. However, I believe all of them ought to be reviewed from time to time by Parliament to see if they perform any useful, democratic, social or economic function in our society.
Some appointments are obviously necessary because the will of Parliament in the form of legislation has to be carried out. However, there must absolutely be a requirement for competence in the job. The person must meet the qualifications. That is what the McGrath report said. It referred to:
-the appointment of the best people possible, and that means appointments
must be more than political patronage.
I agree. Collecting a few bucks for a political Party does not qualify you for just any government job. Soothing the Prime Minister's ego from time to time when he is feeling a bit insecure does not make you fit for any task the Government may have at hand. Serving a Minister for a little while as an adviser, speech writer or "gofer" does not provide you with the wherewithal for just any government assignment.
I do not know if I have time for an illustration but one comes readily to mind. There was a university professor who had a part-time position on a commission. He was highly qualified in that area. It was a part-time position but he could spend as much time as he liked on it, so he gave more and more of his time to it and served extremely well. He was promised by the Minister of the day that when a full-time position came open he would get it. So he reduced his teaching load, served more and more time on the commission, and what happened? An election came along and a Member of Parliament who did not have a hope of winning his seat but had a few brownie points with the Prime Minister got the job. To the best of my knowledge he did not have the faintest idea about
October 6, 1987

the area in which he was now going to be serving the Government for an extended period of time.
I recall rather more recently that an individual from my constituency was called before a committee because he was being appointed to a human rights tribunal. It was an embarrassment, a joke. He did not even understand the basic tenets or underlying principles of human rights, or the legislation we put in place, or his job at the Human Rights Commission. He did not have a clue. Yet the Government brought that man forward and wasted the time of the committee. I might tell my hon. friend from Thunder Bay that even though it was a joke and this person's responses were ludicrous, he got the job.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE ADMINISTRATION ADVISABILITY OF ESTABLISHING PARLIAMENTARY REVIEW OF GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL APPOINTMENTS
speechtext: Shameful.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE ADMINISTRATION ADVISABILITY OF ESTABLISHING PARLIAMENTARY REVIEW OF GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL APPOINTMENTS
speechtext:
Of course it is shameful. That is the kind of thing that goes on.
My friend from Selkirk-Interlake would like us to believe we have made great strides in parliamentary reform. We know we have not because the basis of parliamentary reform is the question: How do we begin to exercise some degree of control over the executive branch of Government? That is what parliamentary reform is all about. How do we begin to restrict the almost unlimited power of a Prime Minister regardless of which political Party he leads? A democracy needs its checks and balances. Under the Constitution Act, 1982 we gave some powers to the Supreme Court. We created a Charter of Rights and Freedoms. We moved in the direction of limiting the powers of the executive.
The McGrath report wanted to do the very same thing for Members of Parliament. It wanted to make them more effective. However, those recommendations have earned a very limited amount of success. I know that government Members want to make much of it, but I think they know in their heart of hearts that making much of how that report was implemented is more propaganda than reality.
We know that the will of the Prime Minister, when he has a majority, virtually becomes law. We have seen that in recent days. For example, when the Meech Lake Accord was brought to this House it was described as a seamless web into which you could not introduce the smallest amendment. The process involving the Constitution committee was meaningless because nothing could be changed. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mul-roney) and his Senate spokesman laid down the law, and this was to remain intact, as it has. Of course we have the same thing in the free trade agreement. We cannot modify it in any way at all. It will go forward as it is.
I will conclude by asking: Why does Parliament exist? We exist mainly to make government accountable for all of its actions; its expenditures, its policies, its programs, and its appointments which we are debating today. This must be real rather than only an illusion. I believe that this national forum will lose the respect of the citizenry unless we carry out this very important function. Has this institution already lost the respect of our citizenry? Lord Acton's dictum, known by most
Governor in Council Appointments
first-year university history students, is: Power corrupts and if that power is absolute it corrupts absolutely.
There must be accountability in every respect. I do not believe, as the Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon would have us believe, that Question Period is accountability. You and I, Sir, know that that is political theatre. Real accountability could take place in committee. However, it will only take place when we actually start making amendments to legislation based on the public hearing process, when we actually turn down some expenditures and make recommendations for other expenditures, and when we say that we will not accept certain appointments because the people are not the best candidates and are not competent.
I support that which the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay- Nipigon has done. The job of parliamentary reform has only just begun.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE ADMINISTRATION ADVISABILITY OF ESTABLISHING PARLIAMENTARY REVIEW OF GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL APPOINTMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a former member of the Special Committee on Reform of the House of Commons, it gives me pleasure today to speak on motion M-39 standing in the name of the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Epp).
I believe that the Hon. Member should have decided today simply to withdraw his motion since the Government has responded favourably to the recommendations of the Committee about the review of Order in Council appointments.
For the benefit of those who will read the proceedings on this motion in Hansard, I would like to quote Standing Order 104(2), which states the following:
The committee-
-that is the Standing Committee of the House having the authority to review an appointment made, for instance, in the area of employment and immigration-
-if it should call an appointee or nominee to appear pursuant to section (1)
of this Standing Order, shall examine the qualifications and competence of the
appointee or nominee to perform the duties of the post to which he or she-
-and the word "e//e" should have been added in the French version-
-has been appointed or nominated.
Mr. Speaker, as Parliamentarians, whatever side of the House we may sit on, I believe that we must admit that the Progressive Conservative Government has made a tremondous step in reforming our institution, precisely in this area of review of Order in Council appointments.
We could say that it is not enough. We could say that we should do even more. However, we must also avoid excess. We have to remember that it is not easy for the members of a Standing Committee to judge totally the qualifications and competence of a person appointed by the Prime Minister of Canada.

October 6, 1987
Governor in Council Appointments
It must also be said that this Standing Order prevents those who make appointments from making bad ones.
Mr. Speaker, knowing quite well that I, as a Canadian, could be appointed to a management position with a Crown Corporation and that I have no special qualifications in that area, I think I would be very uncomfortable about accepting this kind of appointment, because I might be called before a standing committee of the House to explain to committee members what my qualifications are. Mr. Speaker, I think this prevents a lot of bad appointments, and I think we must recognize here the leadership of the Prime Minister who has been very much involved in this parliamentary reform.
Mr. Speaker, I remember when the Hon. Member for St. John's East spoke to the House about the committee's report. The Prime Minister came to the House especially to listen to what the Hon. Member for St. John's East had to say, because the appointment issue was of particular interest to him.
Mr. Speaker, I was listening earlier to the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner). He was also involved, though indirectly, because of his particular interest in parliamentary reform. He came before the committee two or three times, and he is well aware the issue of Order in Council appointments was very important and was given thorough consideration. We looked at all the options in this respect.
Obviously, we had to make some concessions. Mr. Speaker, when 1 heard the Hon. Member who presented his motion today say: Mr. Speaker, partisan appointments are being made here in Canada and this is terrible, and so forth, I felt the Hon. Member was speaking on behalf of a political party that will never sit on the Government side, because after all, one has to be realistic in a democratic party system. When a Progressive Conservative Government is in power, it practically has an obligation to appoint people who support its policies.
The Hon. Member for the New Democratic Party would be in trouble if some day they were to form the Government. Can you imagine New Democrats appointing a known Conservative as head of a Crown Corporation or chairman of a committee? Mr. Speaker, I think it would be rather funny to see how that would work out. After all, one must be realistic.
So I think we can say that Members of this House should constantly, on an annual basis, reflect on the rules by which we are guided, and also on other areas that concern a Member's daily life. I think we can also say that since the reform of our Standing Orders, there has been considerable improvement. Nothing is perfect, of course. Often, everything has to be reviewed every five, ten, fifteen or 20 years. This is a changing world with changing concepts, and I would say that perhaps we would have to review everything on an annual basis.
As Members from all sides of this House, we should ask questions and re-evaluate ourselves and our rules. I quite agree with the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Epp) and the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior that as Members we are in a position to review these issues.
Mr. Speaker, I would also like to point out that the right to veto an appointment suggested by the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon seems to be a bit arbitrary. After all, veto rights or the right to appoint... Mr. Speaker, quite frankly, after my work on the standing committee and after hearing witnesses address the issue of reviewing Order in Council appointments, 1 have no hesitation in saying that I would not like to be in a position where, as a Member, 1 would have to select two or three people out of a pool of 1,000 in my riding with the ability, intelligence and qualifications to sit on Government commissions.
I would rather have these appointments made by the Prime Minister so as to avoid finding myself in an embarrassing situation in the eyes of my own constituents. In fact, Mr. Speaker, I am sure my colleague would agree that House of Commons Standing Orders 103 and 104 answer these questions and meet all expectations. If he agrees with me he will admit that our Government has covered a lot of ground in that respect and that, for the time being, his motion is not justified and should simply be dropped from the Order Paper because the Government did respond to this question of order in council appointments.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE ADMINISTRATION ADVISABILITY OF ESTABLISHING PARLIAMENTARY REVIEW OF GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL APPOINTMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 only intend to speak for five minutes in order to allow the Hon. Member for London East (Mr. Jepson) to speak. I want to deal with what has happened with respect to the whole question of reviewing appointments.
The House will recall that early in the term of this Government there was a great controversy about appointments and the perception and reality of patronage in those appointments. The response of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) was that this was a matter with which the Special Committee on the Reform of the House of Commons would deal. That committee was sometimes referred to as the McGrath committee. For some six months, the Prime Minister, in what I believe was a rather politically deft move, was able to say, when asked about patronage, that this matter was referred to the committee headed by the former Member for St. John's East. He would go on to say that he was looking forward to the recommendations of the committee and so on.
When the report of the Special Committee on the Reform of the House of Commons finally came forward, it recommended neither what the Prime Minister eventually instituted nor a procedure as wide ranging as that proposed by the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Epp) in his motion. It recommended that there be a review and veto power only with respect to positions on quasi-judicial bodies, such as the CRTC, the CTC, the NEB and officers of the House of Commons, and that there be a review procedure but no veto power with respect to the rest of the appointments.
October 6, 1987

I still believe that this was a nice compromise because, pursuant to some of the remarks made by the Prime Minister, it would have been an opportunity for parliamentarians to exercise some real but nevertheless limited power over appointments.
Again, I think the Prime Minister made another politically deft move by saying that all appointments will be open to review, without being open to veto. This has resulted in the same situation as exists in the American system, even though they have more veto power. Since everything is open to review, nothing is open to review. There are so many appointments that no one can possibly review them all. Therefore, the only appointments that are reviewed are those which have a certain political notoriety.
That is not what the committee intended. It wanted to involve Members of Parliament in some meaningful consideration of appointments.
I am not saying this for politically partisan purposes, because 1 believe that an objective analysis shows that we have ended up with nothing. There is a review process that is never exercised except in a highly political context, which presumably is something no one had in mind.
I return to the original recommendations of the committee. I would like the Government to reconsider providing for a review and veto power on a limited number of appointments, which we believe would not call into question the basic constitutional notion of the Crown's ability to appoint because of the nature of these bodies, and to leave the review possibility in place for all other appointments. In that way there could be a real test of the role parliamentarians could play in appointments. We have not had that test and will not see one under the current rules.
I thank the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon for raising the matter and giving me an opportunity as a member of that committee to comment on the progress of that recommendation. I do not think it has progressed very well.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE ADMINISTRATION ADVISABILITY OF ESTABLISHING PARLIAMENTARY REVIEW OF GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL APPOINTMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to add my own comments to this debate on the motion proposed by the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Epp) concerning the process of House committee review of governor In council appointments.
Under this process, which has been in place for roughly a year and a half now, the Government is required to table in the House the Orders in Council of almost all individuals whom it appoints. There are some exceptions, such as judges, and these exceptions are completely justifiable.
According to the Standing Orders on this process, specifically Standing Order 103(2), a Minister of the Crown on behalf of the Government may also, from time to time, table a certificate stating that a specified individual has been nominated for appointment to a specified non-judicial post.
Governor in Council Appointments
The Government has two ways to bring people forward for consideration by House committees. They are: as appointees who have been appointed; and for three regulatory agencies, the CRTC, the CTC and the NEB, as nominees whom it has not yet appointed.
The Government has tabled hundreds of appointments in this House, and a number of certificates of nominations. Let me give some recent examples. There are appointments to boards established under federal legislation such as the Farm Debt Review Board, boards of referees of the Unemployment Insurance Commission, National Parole Board, and Atomic Energy Control Board. There are appointments to the boards of Crown corporations, such as VIA Rail, the Canadian Commercial Corporation, and Telesat Canada. There are appointments to agencies such as the Medical Research Council, the Science Council, and the Advisory Council on the Status of Women. Recently, a new director of the National Gallery of Canada was appointed. There are citizenship judges, because these, in fact, do not have judicial powers. The names of senior public servants such as ambassadorial appointments, and of the new Deputy Superintendent of Financial Institutions have recently been tabled. There was a recent nomination to the Canadian Radio-Television and Telecommunications Commission.
The names of all the above individuals and many others appointed or nominated are tabled in the House and referred to an appropriate standing committee, which then has the opportunity within 30 sitting days to call that individual to appear.
As Members know, a hearing is not mandatory. Standing committees do not call many of the individuals which the Government appoints or nominates for a committee hearing. However, a number of people have been invited to appear by various committees, including appointees to the Bank of Canada, who were the first to be called, and others including a number of senior public servants.
In no case to date, however, has a House committee reported to the House that a government appointee or nominee was not qualified or competent to perform the duties of the post to which he or she was appointed or nominated.
The record indicates that the people appointed by the Government are not unqualified recipients of political reward. We are not talking here about patronage. Rather, we are seeing proof of the Government's record in appointing qualified, competent individuals seriously interested and prepared to serve Canada in the many positions which it is the Government's responsibility to fill.
This review process is a good reform which I am sure all Members will continue to support. While all of us would agree that the new reform is not perfect, it is a giant step forward when one reflects on what has existed in the past. The Government has received criticism for not being open and honest with the people, yet the reforms we have undertaken are

October 6, 1987
Adjournment Debate
clearly a breath of fresh air compared to what we faced in the past.
As a member of the Justice Committee, I know nominees have appeared before the committees with their resumes. There has been opportunity for the committee to call these people should it wish to interview them. It is obvious that the people whom we have put forward are very competent individuals for these posts and the committee has clearly not seen fit to bring them forward for specific interviews.
I believe we are encouraged by this reform. We admit that it is not perfect, but it is a giant step forward from what we experienced in the past.

OF MANITOBA REGION/DEPARTMENT'S SERVICE TO INDIAN PEOPLE

Mr. Speaker, there is a serious problem in the Province of Manitoba regarding the Department of Indian Affairs. This unresolved problem is having some very drastic consequences for the lives of Indian people and the communities in which they live.
First, let me be very clear to you, Mr. Speaker, about the nature of the problem. It is not one of fraud, nor one of dishonesty, per se, nor of gross negligence. It is one of serious mismanagement.
Second, it is my firm conviction, and this is supported by concerns expressed by the previous Minister, the Hon. Member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie), that the Manitoba problem of serious mismanagement in the Department of Indian Affairs is widespread.
Third, it is not my intention to disparage or to lash out against officials in the Department in Manitoba, or in any other region of the Department of Indian Affairs. I believe
they are caught in an intolerable and unacceptable position. They are being squeezed like lemons.
The real problem is the Minister himself and the senior bureaucrats who direct and pull him around, plus all of the excess and the overlay and the paraphernalia of the headquarters of the Department of Indian Affairs here in Ottawa. To put it simply and bluntly, the mentality toward Indian people by the Minister and his senior bureaucrats is that they are no more than wards of the state; they cannot be trusted nor relied upon to control, regulate or manage their own affairs. I know that in public fora, in conferences and the like the Minister and senior bureaucrats may talk about aboriginal selfgovernment, but they do not really believe it at all. What they believe in, is doing what has to be done under the Indian Act, and doing it their way.
The Coopers & Lybrand report about the Manitoba situation put it very well, and I quote, "The fact is that most existing instructions were issued at a time when the Department was seeking to strengthen controls in responding to criticisms of the Auditor General". I believe that the senior bureaucrats in the Department really took pleasure and delight in the Auditor General's criticisms because it meant that they could tighten down the screws, that they could run a tight ship, that they could put those Indians in their place.
But, on the other side, there was something else which they had to take into account. That was the demand and the pressure for self-government. It was becoming too much to keep the lid on, and they had to do something.
So we have a problem, Sir, that in addition to those financial instructions that were issued by the Department there also went out laterally some vague and weak directives regarding, first, contribution agreements, and, second, something called alternative funding arrangements. So we now have it. The stage is now set for serious mismanagement. What a dark and tragic theatre it is. I say that because people's lives are involved, as is their education, the care of their children, their housing, social services, and so on.
So, first, we have the Treasury Board terms and conditions of 1979. This leads to continuous monitoring of Indian use of funds by Department officials to ensure compliance that all the terms and conditions are met. This is why in Manitoba, where most services are actually carried out by Indian people, there are now more civil servants than there were in the past. What are they doing? They are busy monitoring, keeping a watchful eye over the entire process.
Second, and following up on this monitoring, we have the control accounting system which fully satisfies the region's needs for financial control but which completely fails to analyse expenditures of benefit to Indians or tribal councils. Now, to further complicate the situation in Manitoba, there are program managers. They are closer to the Indian people themselves, to the bands and the tribal councils. In the interests of Indian people with whom they relate directly, these program managers sometimes, according to Coopers &
October 6, 1987

Lybrand, circumvent financial controls to make the best and maximum use of financial funds. In other words, Sir, they bend financial rules in order to satisfy what they believe to be the legitimate needs of the Indian people whom they are called upon to help.
The financial staff of the Department enter the picture much later, that is after these decisions have been made, and so many of their precious instructions have already been broken.
What is the result? The result is a mess. It is serious mismanagement. If time allows me, I will tell you what the answer is as quickly as I can.
Number one, we need a new Government. If we wish to down size the Department, do it here in Ottawa, not out in the field where they are actually trying to serve people. We need a clear policy on aboriginal self-government. It is an inherent and inalienable right and it should be exercised. We need the recommendation of the special committee to be accepted; that, in terms of financing, we need block funding agreements on a multi-year basis. Finally, we need to purge from our system the notion that Indian people are incapable and unable to govern themselves. Of course they are, and they will do it much better than many of the forms of self-government that we see around this country, whether they be municipalities, certain provinces, or do I need to look any further than right across the floor.
