speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with regard to the concerns raised by the Hon. Member, it was the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development who, in October, 1986, required the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to investigate the allegations of wrongdoing. Further, he requested that the President of the Treasury Board undertake a comprehensive review of the financial operations of the Department's regional office in Manitoba. Those actions were taken because he was committed to ensuring that sound financial practices were in place throughout the Department.
The comprehensive review of financial operations of the Manitoba region was undertaken by the Office of the Comptroller General with the assistance of Coopers & Lybrand Consulting Group. That review examined the region's financial management practices, including resource allocation, administration, monitoring and reporting, with specific attention to the administration of contribution agreements and contracts. The Minister released the findings of the report in September, 1987.
After careful review of the report, I am pleased to note that it did not uncover a single case of wilful wrongdoing on the part of the Department's employees. Furthermore, as the Minister indicated to the House on September 22, the report concluded that, "Although the region satisfactorily complies
Adjournment Debate
with most parliamentary and government policies and requirements where it delivers services directly to Indians, it fails to fully comply with these policies and requirements where administrative responsibilities have been devolved to Indian bands, tribal councils or their representatives".
In the consultant's opinion this situation has arisen, "Because the Department's clientele do not believe that these policies and practices are appropriate where they have assumed delivery or administrative responsibilities and the region is unwilling to enforce compliance by withholding funding to which the Indian bands are entitled".
Departmental officials are currently doing a detailed analysis of the findings of the report and will be working with the Comptroller General to complete, within two or three months, an action plan that addresses all the deficiencies identified in the report.
I can assure you that the Department of Indian and Northern Affairs is in the process of introducing a financial management regime that is consistent with and supportive of the Government's thrust to transfer the administration of programs and the associated funding to Indian Governments.
ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-POLITICAL RESPONSIBILITY-MINISTER'S POSITION/RESPONS1BILITY FOR ACTIONS OF RCMP

Mr. Speaker, for a few weeks now, the Hon. Member for York South-Weston (Mr. Nunziata) and I have been asking questions designed to demonstrate-and I think we have demonstrated it-that the Government is not accountable for the way in which the national security operations of the country are being handled.
We are very critical of a number of things which have visibly gone wrong. We have no sense, in the answers which we are getting from across the floor, that the Solicitor General (Mr. Kelleher) in particular has any recognition of how serious the problems are or, indeed, that he has come to grips with them and is planning to do anything about them.
Three years ago, when this Government took office, it was exactly the moment of the launching of the new Canadian Security Intelligence Service, which was created by legislation and passed in the last weeks of the life of the former Government. This Government took over the tremendous responsibility of organizing the launch of CSIS, which was responsible for providing intelligence to the Government about threats to the national security as defined in that Act.
We know from all the evidence we have that a great number of things have gone wrong within the operations of the Canadian Security Intelligence Service in terms of its relationship with the RCMP and in terms of defining what is its mandate.
I put it to the Minister that he should take responsibility for that service as the statute requires him to do, recognize the

October 6, 1987
Adjournment Debate
problems, and take on the first fundamental responsibility of telling the Canadian Security Intelligence Service what is the product the Government wants it to produce and how the responsibility in the area is to be shared with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
I feel that time after time the problems which are surfacing are the result of a Government that is standing back and asking the RCMP and the new agency, the Canadian Security Intelligence Service, to settle their own differences through liaison and through co-operation. That is no way for the Minister to take responsibility for the Department.
The RCMP is so well established, is so large, has such a large budget, and has such a clear level of support among the Canadian people that getting the Canadian Security Intelligence Service launched requires the Minister to be present, to be giving directions, and to be making decisions. When matters are left to the two agencies to settle, I fear that in every case the decision will go to the RCMP just because of its greater ascendency, so the Canadian Security Intelligence Service is not being properly launched and properly supported to do the very important work that it must do.
There was evidence of that last week when Doug Roche, who has some responsibility for awarding public money to peace groups, said that, yes, the Canadian Security Intelligence Service occasionally gives them some advice about which peace groups have been targeted, supported, and manipulated by, for example, foreign Governments or subversive elements. However, Mr. Roche said: "We didn't ask for that advice and we don't take that into consideration".
What kind of signal is that to give to the CSIS about its work? Either the Government wants it to be doing that job, or the Government should tell it not to do it. It should not allow it to do it and then dump on it, through the lips of Doug Roche, one of Canada's Ambassadors, and say that what it does is not wanted and no account is taken of it.
Last week we on this side of the House, in both Parties, pressed the Minister for taking some responsibility for the infiltration which may have occurred by members of the Canadian Security Intelligence Service into the peace movement and the union movement to see whether he supported it. He said, and I am quoting him exactly: "I have no evidence that the Canadian Security Intelligence Service has exceeded its mandate".
That is not a good enough answer. The Minister should have been in a position to say "I am satisfied that they are not exceeding their mandate", or he should have said "there is a problem here and this is what I am doing to try to solve it".
For him to say "I have no evidence" and then to tell any Members of the House or indeed any Canadians who have evidence that the Canadian Security Intelligence Service is exceeding its mandate, targeting people who are not threats to the security of Canada, that they should take that information to the Service is a total dereliction of his duty. The irony is
that the Canadian Security Intelligence Service was examined by the Security Intelligence Review Committee.
This Security Intelligence Review Committee has expressed concern that the service is exceeding its mandate. For the Minister to tell us to take our complaints to the SIRC, which is already concerned about the service exceeding its mandate, simply shows that the Minister is not responsible, that he is not taking the fundamental responsibility for his agency, giving it the necessary directions and finding out what it is doing.
I want to express the total lack of confidence of the Official Opposition in the way this Minister has been passing the buck and sending us to SIRC. In one other circumstance, the Minister told us that the Director of the Canadian Security Intelligence Service is responsible for the agency and, because things were going wrong in the agency, the Director offered his resignation and the Minister accepted it. That was satisfactory as far as the Minister was concerned. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) indicated as well that the Canadian Security Intelligence Service is an independent agency and that its Director had done the honourable thing because of what had gone wrong and had resigned. That was not at all the proper way for the issue to be handled. The agency is not an independent agency. It is, in fact, by definition and by law a dependant agency. The Minister is accountable 100 per cent for its operations. There is no way in our tradition that a Deputy Minister's resignation should have been asked for, condoned and accepted. If anyone should have resigned, it should have been the Minister.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I would like to point out that the Minister has fully responded to the questions just bootlegged into this debate by my hon. friend.
I would like to respond to the question raised by my colleague on September 22, 1987, which was supposed to be the subject for debate at this time, namely, the RCMP witness/informant protection. Despite the fact that the issue raised by my hon. friend on September 22 is sub judice, I would like to assure the Members of this House that the protection of witnesses and informants has been a particular concern of the Solicitor General (Mr. Kelleher). I would like to take this opportunity to outline the steps that he has taken in this regard. The Solicitor General has had a thorough review conducted of witness/informant protection arrangements, and I would like to describe some of the key features of the RCMP program.
First, investigators are provided detailed and very explicit instructions on how sources are to be handled, particularly with regard to limitations on the commitments that can be given to the informants at the investigation level. Second, informants are compensated on the basis of the value of the their informational services performed to advance the investigation of the offence. Third, the RCMP provides protection to
October 6, 1987

such individuals and their immediate families when there is clear evidence that they have been, or are likely to be, seriously threatened as a result of acting as an RCMP informant. Finally, as an aspect of protection, informants and their families may be provided with a range of services including relocation in another city, change of identity and financial support.
The RCMP has a comprehensive and effective witness/infor-mant protection program which is sensitive to the genuine requirements of these individuals and their families. I can assure the Members of this House that it is both fair and just.
The Hon. Member will appreciate that the use of informants is a necessary, in fact crucial aspect of many police investigations, particularly those which involve organized criminal conspiracies. Given the size of the RCMP and the complexity of the investigations the RCMP are charged to undertake, it is reasonable to conclude that the force deals with many informants on an ongoing basis, otherwise it would not be the very successful police force that it clearly is. In such circumstances, it is not surprising that from time to time, an informant is not satisfied with the treatment he or she is afforded. In such cases, the individual can, of course, under our system of justice, seek remedies through a civil proceeding. The important point here is that such occurrences are extremely rare given the many informants handled by the RCMP.
I would also like to remind the Hon. Member that police work is always very difficult and at times thankless. The RCMP are being asked to respond to a range of infinite social problems in the communities with finite resources. Increasingly, they are being required to undertake complex investigations under extreme pressure. I believe the Members of the House owe a vote of confidence to the loyalty and dedication of these men and women who serve their communities and their country in such an exemplary manner.

Mr. Speaker, I know that I do not have to remind you that since the Young Offenders Act was introduced into the House and passed into law by the former Liberal Government, it has been a very, very controversial piece of legislation. You know as well as I do, Mr. Speaker, that the Young Offenders Act replaced the former Juvenile Delinquents Act. It became effective law prior to the election of our Government, but it did not actually take effect as law of the land until after the Government was elected in the spring of 1985.
Almost immediately when it went into effect, the law was highly criticized, particularly by police forces, and particularly by police forces in the Province of Ontario. Following that criticism, the then Solicitor General who was at that time in charge of Young Offenders Act legislation, the Hon. Minister of National Defence (Mr. Beatty), commenced consultations with his colleagues right across Canada for the purpose of
Adjournment Debate
determining whether or not changes should be made to the Act.
Following those consultations, in fact changes were introduced in the House and passed into law but in spite of those changes, not all of the criticisms have disappeared. I suppose if I could identify one particular criticism that keeps coming up more and more often, it is the issue of those under twelve years of age, the minimum age at which the Young Offenders Act takes effect.
Prior to the introduction and passage of the Young Offenders Act, the age for criminal responsibility was seven years old. In fact, seven-year-olds and those older were subject to the Juvenile Delinquents Act. At the same time as the Young Offenders Act was introduced and passed, the Criminal Code was amended to remove the age of seven as the age of criminal responsibility. In fact, the age became 12, the minimum age dealt with in the Young Offenders Act.
It was anticipated at the time that each one of the provinces of Canada would put in place child welfare legislation which would deal with those young people from seven years of age to 12 years of age and that that would be the effective way of dealing with young people in that age bracket who were offenders. Unfortunately, that has not really come to pass.
While child welfare legislation has been put in place, the controversy continues to rage over whether that should be the effective way of dealing with children under 12 who are involved in criminal offences or if we should not lower the age in the Young Offenders Act.
I have raised in the House on occasion the fact that in Metro Toronto in 1985, 1,855 children under 12 were involved in very serious offences; 41 of them were involved in arson cases, 11 in sexual assaults and 15 in weapons incidents. That has prompted the Attorney General of the Province of Ontario to indicate that despite the existence of the child welfare system, there is a need for a safety net of criminal law. Otherwise, he says, there is no deterrent to criminal behaviour by children under the age of 12.
As you know, the Hon. Ian Scott, Attorney General of the Province of Ontario, has been criticized by Attorneys General in other provinces for that statement. They indicated that what the Province of Ontario really needs is stronger child welfare legislation, not amendments to the Young Offenders Act, It was indicated, for instance, that in the Province of Quebec that is the case and that deals with the problem effectively.
At the end of May of this year our Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn), now charged with the responsibility for this legislation, met with his provincial counterparts and discussed this problem, among many others. In early June of this year I asked that Minister in this House whether he was prepared to make further amendments dealing with the minimum age in the Young Offenders Act, or whether he was going to leave it

October 6, 1987
Adjournment Debate
to child welfare legislation to deal with the problem. The Minister said his officials and provincial officials were going to be meeting to study the problem.
Four months have now passed by and surely it is not unreasonable to expect a response from the Government. Will it tell us tonight one way or another: Is it going to change the Young Offenders Act and reduce the age of responsibility from twelve to seven or perhaps somewhere in between? Or, is it going to do nothing and rely strictly and solely on child welfare legislation to deal with this problem?

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Shields (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to say at the outset that it is a pleasure to share the House this evening at this hour of debate with my hon. colleague from York East. I know he has displayed considerable interest in this distinct problem facing the judicial system and young people.
The minimum age of 12 was established during the process leading to the introduction and passage, in 1982, of the Young Offenders Act. 1 am sure he is aware of that. There was then a general consensus that the age of seven was simply not reflective of the policies or daily practices of the juvenile justice system. It was decided, as was the case under the Juvenile Delinquents Act, that children who threatened to harm themselves or others are best dealt with through provincial child welfare legislation. This enables authorities to apprehend children and provide special care and treatment for them and their families.
While the very young cannot be dealt with by means of criminal prosecution, it is in society's interest that they and their families be helped through formal family and children's services.
The issue of minimum age was raised during the consultations preceding Bill C-106 when changes were vigorously urged by some observers. The Hon. Member indicated he was one of those vigorous observers. For most participating in those consultations, however, it was not an issue requiring immediate attention and proposals of change also were opposed with vigour.
At the recent meeting of federal and provincial Ministers responsible for juvenile justice, the adequacy of child welfare legislation to deal with offences committed by children under the age of 12 was discussed. As indicated earlier, the Ministers did not reach a consensus on the proposition put forward by the Attorney General of Ontario. However, it was agreed that there was a need to ensure and maintain the capacity to respond effectively to anti-social behaviour of these children.
This issue has been referred to officials to ensure that the appropriate mechanism to respond to the needs of these children and to protect society is available.
